Their sum is 100 resources, not 100 skill lessons: the schedule includes a motivation break and a feedback survey. The conditional ledger above preserves all 54 observed URLs in order, excluding the duplicated featured Last viewed card.\\r\\n\\r\\nFormal argument resources appear before and after indicator practice: conditional argument and symbolic translation first, contraposition next, and chaining later. The combined-arguments lesson and review follow the chaining sets. This order is observed; its pedagogical rationale is inferred unless the inspected teaching states it. A title describes topic scope; it does not by itself prove the full teaching content was reviewed.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Translation and chaining receive repeated practice\\r\\n\\r\\nThe inspected Logic of an Argument article distinguishes a valid/invalid formal relationship from the continuum of strength in informal reasoning. The inspected sets lesson uses circles and dots, nested sets and relative subset/superset roles. It warns through membership reasoning that being outside one category does not determine the alternative category. These foundations precede notation and indicator drills, so the sequence introduces meaning before repeated translation. That final relationship is an interpretation of observed order.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe parent\'s page inspection found a four-step Group 2 translation procedure: identify the indicator, identify the main concepts, assign symbols, and apply the rule. Contraposing and translating back into ordinary language are optional follow-through moves. The article contrasts sufficient and necessary conditions and valid ways to use a rule, helping prevent an unsupported reverse inference. These are inspected written teaching findings, not claims that its video was fully watched.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe Group 1 worksheet has five prompts. Its Answer controls reveal both the diagram and its contrapositive. That feedback asks the learner to check equivalence and direction, rather than checking only a memorized indicator label. No answers were submitted or worksheet completion recorded during research.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe schedule places **four translation sets estimated at 30 minutes each after Group 2**, while the other indicator groups have **one 30-minute set each**. Inspection shows these four sets are cumulative **Group 1 and Group 2** retrieval, not Group 2-only training. Each contains five prompts. Group 1, Group 3 and Group 4 each also have five prompts. Thus the seven translation worksheets provide thirty-five prompts and 210 estimated practice minutes; twenty of those prompts and 120 minutes occur in the cumulative block after Group 2. Chaining has two five-prompt sets estimated at forty minutes each: ten prompts and eighty minutes. These are schedule estimates, not video runtimes or actual learner times.\\r\\n\\r\\nAn inferred rationale is to consolidate both positive indicator groups through varied syntax before adding negative translation rules. The cumulative worksheets include universal language, only/only-if/only-when/only-where, modifiers, embedded attribution and longer scoped concepts. This is evidence of deliberate variation and cumulative retrieval; it does not establish four times as much necessary-condition practice. LSAT U should audit actual error patterns before copying the time allocation.\\r\\n\\r\\n## What the inspected written teaching does step by step\\r\\n\\r\\nThese original summaries reflect the parent\'s inspected written pages. They do not imply that embedded videos were watched. Number references correspond to the ordered source links above.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Resources | Inspected teaching and training purpose | Transition or limit |\\r\\n|---|---|---|\\r\\n| 4–6: sets and sufficiency/necessity | Membership in a sufficient subset implies membership in the necessary superset; failing the necessary condition excludes the sufficient subset. The same group can occupy different relational roles within a chain. Circles, dots and nesting make those relationships visible. | Builds relational meaning before symbols. Relative roles prevent treating sufficient/necessary as permanent labels for a term. |\\r\\n| 7: conditional argument | Separates a conditional rule from a supplied fact, then uses the fact to apply the rule forward. | Gives a first formal application. The rule alone does not establish its trigger. |\\r\\n| 8: truth and validity | Asks the learner to grant the premises for the validity check, even when their factual content is false. | Separates logical consequence from factual plausibility. |\\r\\n| 9–10: Lawgic and translation | Arrows reduce distraction from content. Translation separates the rule from an individual\'s membership fact. | Introduces notation as a representation of already-understood reasoning, not a substitute for comprehension. |\\r\\n| 11: sets versus conditions | Distinguishes categorical membership from events while treating the shared inference form as useful for LSAT work. | Supports transfer between different surface wording. Do not erase semantic differences merely because notation overlaps. |\\r\\n| 12: negation | Distinguishes contradiction from an ordinary opposite and explains double negation. | Prepares the sign changes in contraposition and later compound negation. |\\r\\n| 13–14: contrapositive and argument #2 | Flip direction and negate both conditions to obtain an equivalent rule. A fact denying the necessary condition excludes the sufficient condition. | Teaches a second valid application, rather than an unsupported reversal. |\\r\\n| 15: legal transfer | An edited legal argument illustrates contraposition and highlights a possible hidden semantic assumption. | Transfer still needs interpretation of the actual claims; formal notation does not settle a missing substantive assumption. |\\r\\n| 17–18: English expressions and indicators | Several English forms can express one relationship. Indicator words can be overinclusive or incomplete guides; context determines whether a guarantee is actually present. Not every occurrence of when creates a conditional. | Prevents keyword-only reasoning before four-group practice. |\\r\\n| 19: Group 1 | Four steps: detect the indicator, parse the concepts, assign symbols and apply the translation rule. Contrapose/retranslate optionally. Grammar and economical notation require attention. | Rehearses a process rather than simple word recognition. |\\r\\n| 21: Group 2 | Uses the same procedure for necessary indicators and contrasts sufficient/necessary relationships with valid applications. | Additional scheduled practice targets the direction-sensitive language. The rationale for exact weighting remains inferred. |\\r\\n| 26–27: Group 3 and Or | Negating either complete idea as sufficient can produce equivalent contrapositive forms; retranslation checks meaning. The Or lesson distinguishes inclusive, exclusive and contextual either meanings. | Compound and ordinary-language scope matter beyond a fixed unless recipe. |\\r\\n| 29 and 31: Group 4 and summary | Negate either idea as necessary, then consolidate the four indicator groups. | Group labels support translation; they do not replace checking the complete statement. |\\r\\n| 34: chaining | Demonstrates symbolic and English chains, including four-node chains, multiple supported conclusions and contrapositives. | Extends two-rule connections to intermediate and end-to-end inferences. |\\r\\n| 37–38: combine and review | A valid-conclusion exercise is followed by an invalid argument, exposing why satisfying the necessary condition or failing the sufficient condition gives no forced conclusion. | Integrates the three formal argument forms with tempting invalid moves. |\\r\\n| 39: FAQ | Presents diagrams as a strategic option. Slow deliberate practice builds intuition; revisit it and diagram on the test when complexity makes the notation useful. | Does not prescribe compulsory diagrams for every question. Source numerical frequency claims are not treated as verified test statistics. |\\r\\n| 43: without indicators | Active/passive guarantees and requirement grammar can represent the same rule. Modifiers define the relevant subject subset. The lesson discourages extending memorized word lists indefinitely. | Returns from indicator recognition to semantic parsing. |\\r\\n| 44 and 46: conjunction/disjunction | An AND antecedent requires the joint condition and cannot generally split; an AND consequent can. An OR consequent does not force a particular branch; an OR antecedent can split into separate rules. | Scope determines which decomposition is valid. Teach the operation with its position, not the connective alone. |\\r\\n| 47: De Morgan | Negate the entire compound, swap its connective, negate each component and cancel double negations; restore the contrapositive relationship. | Depends on whole-claim negation and compound scope. |\\r\\n| 49: domain | Separates scope conditions from the active rule and suggests revisiting this technique in later LR study. | LSAT U must verify membership in the restricted domain before suppressing a condition in notation. A scope simplification is not permission to discard premises. |\\r\\n| 51: biconditionals | Contrasts if and only if, combines two directions, and shows equal truth values and the equivalent negative pair. | Exclusive alternatives connect one claim to the negation of the other; they are not an ordinary same-truth-value biconditional. |\\r\\n\\r\\nThe Sufficiency and Necessity Workshop exposed an embedded circles activity labelled mammals/dogs with a Start control. It was not launched, so its interactions and feedback remain unverified. You Try entrances promise an attempt followed by explanation, but their explanation/feedback screens were not inspected. Their actual transfer feedback remains a gap in this research.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Practice adds cumulative syntax and reasoning demands\\r\\n\\r\\nGroup 3\'s five prompts cover without, unless and until, including an existing negation and a domain restriction. The first Answer reveal was inspected and showed both equivalent directions. Group 4\'s five prompts cover no, none and never with longer modified concepts. Group 1\'s first worksheet reveal likewise showed diagram and contrapositive. Full feedback for every prompt was not individually revealed.\\r\\n\\r\\nEach chaining worksheet has five prompts. Inspection found reordered rules and contraposition, nonconnecting premises, irrelevant information, and a distinction between being expected to do something and being able to do it. The practice therefore tests parsing and whether a link is licensed, rather than merely connecting repeated letters.\\r\\n\\r\\nDraw Valid Conclusions 1 has five prompts asking the learner to translate, combine supported conclusions and translate back. It includes double negation, concrete facts and implicit requirements. The compound worksheet reports five prompts, with at least four directly visible in the inspection slice. Its inspected rationale includes modifiers hiding conjunctions, timing as an extra prerequisite and the distinction between negation and opposition.\\r\\n\\r\\nPre-hydration DOM snapshots can expose hidden answer text and lose negation styling. This research does not diagnose an incorrect answer from plain DOM alone. It relies on inspected semantics and the verified reveal interactions, while preserving the remaining feedback limits.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Preserve the useful distinctions and adjudicate source shortcuts\\r\\n\\r\\nThe inspected Other Conjunction Indicators page treats but, even if and even though as AND. Do not copy that as a universal semantic rewrite. Even if does not establish that its antecedent is true; even though usually presents that clause as a fact. Any LSAT U treatment should distinguish the context-specific logical relationship rather than make a blanket connective substitution.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe domain simplification also needs an explicit boundary: the rule is applicable only after its domain condition is established. Likewise, quantified all-to-most-to-some shorthand requires the relevant existence assumption, addressed in [the quantity analysis](research-7sage-quantifiers.md). These are original analytical cautions, not claims that a title alone proves the source wrong.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe analysis separates these dimensions:\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Skill:** the operation the student learns, based on inspected teaching rather than title alone.\\r\\n- **Prerequisites:** explicitly stated prerequisites separately from inferred dependencies.\\r\\n- **Instruction:** what reasoning is explained, the distinction it makes and any error it rules out.\\r\\n- **Training mechanism:** demonstration, worksheet, classification, derivation, guided attempt or independent check.\\r\\n- **Practice and feedback:** visible task count, what the answer reveal explains, and whether both diagram and contrapositive appear.\\r\\n- **Transition:** how the resource prepares for the next resource; label inference when the platform does not state it.\\r\\n- **Evidence:** text read, answer reveal inspected, video-only/unread audiovisual, or title/order metadata only.\\r\\n\\r\\nNo source example sentences, full captions, transcripts or item banks are copied here. Opening a lesson is not completing it. A title and duration do not establish the depth of teaching.\\r\\n\\r\\n## How to assess relative emphasis\\r\\n\\r\\nThe observed order emphasizes semantic foundations before notation, then positive indicator translation, negative indicator translation, chaining and combined arguments, followed by compound scope and biconditionals. Real-question attempts and adaptive practice punctuate the sequence. Known worksheet time estimates establish a substantial cumulative translation block and a separate chaining block; the other durations are unavailable in this report. A resource can cover several operations, so resource counts are not independent skill counts. Teaching minutes, practice estimates and verified task counts must remain separate.\\r\\n\\r\\nResource order can suggest the platform\'s instructional progression, but it does not prove that every learner must master one before accessing another. State whether sequencing is enforced or simply presented only when inspected.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Original LSAT U coverage proposal from existing local evidence\\r\\n\\r\\nThese are recommendations, not competitor findings or final curriculum decisions. Beginner / Medium / Advanced are broad teaching stages. Each should contain both a complete pathway assignment and independently assignable specific-skill subsections.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Stage | Teach and assess | Existing material to reuse | Content or packaging needed |\\r\\n|---|---|---|---|\\r\\n| Beginner | Rule versus fact; sufficient/necessary; what is forced versus left possible; Group 1/2 translation; simple negation and contraposition; Group 3/4; all four ways a fact can relate to a rule | Refresher cheat sheet/sorting/diagrams; selected General items; MBT lecture opening and fact-triggering applications | Short coherent notes, isolated valid/invalid application practice, specific Group 3 assignment, fresh diagnostic and clear untimed mastery criteria |\\r\\n| Medium | Connect compatible rules; expose links through contraposition; preserve negative links; distinguish shared result from a bridge; find a missing premise; combine a chain with a fact; AND/OR scope | Hub Linking/Missing Link/MBT banks; SA chain exercises; MBT lecture | Separate operations currently mixed together, worked examples with fading scaffolds, no-link contrast items and targeted fresh transfer pools |\\r\\n| Advanced | Nested/compound negation; alternative branches; biconditionals; multiple chains and irrelevant rules; precision under natural-language complexity; transfer across MBT/MSS, SA, principle, parallel and flaw | Harder General items, compound hub questions, SA chapters, guided real-question pools | Operation-level audit, original gaps filled after review, unseen transfer tasks and speed practice after accuracy |\\r\\n| Quantifiers, next phase | Meaning and scope of all/none/some/most; existence assumptions; direction and negation; valid/invalid quantified combinations; mixed quantified/conditional inferences | Partial legacy Some/Most material and MBT scope examples | Dedicated source-backed original lesson sequence and answer-keyed independent practice; confirm prerequisite and placement relative to the three stages |\\r\\n\\r\\nDo not use a single overall percentage as the only placement evidence. Distinguish translation direction, negation, scope, chaining, triggering and application. Successful repetition of an explained question is review evidence; a fresh structurally related item supplies stronger transfer evidence.\\r\\n\\r\\n## A subsection should be a complete learning unit\\r\\n\\r\\nProposed independently assignable subsection structure: a short explanation of one skill, one worked original example, a guided attempt, fresh independent practice, immediate move-specific feedback, and an exit check. The teacher should be able to assign the whole stage or only the failed skill. The student should see why that subsection is next and what would count as readiness to progress.\\r\\n\\r\\nExisting whole-resource assignments, browser-local refresher progress, saved hub practice and General indicator ledgers are different mechanisms. A unified curriculum needs to connect them; it should not silently claim they already form an adaptive mastery pathway.\\r\\n"}'}]

[{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 2.3 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"i":0,"result":{"status":"fulfilled","value":{"chunk_id":"ad799b","wall_time_seconds":1.9935256,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":0,"output":""}}}'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"i":1,"result":{"status":"fulfilled","value":{"chunk_id":"bc9baf","wall_time_seconds":2.1181111,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":12,"output":"Import-Clixml: Root element is missing.\\r\\nFalse\\r\\n"}}}'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"i":2,"result":{"status":"fulfilled","value":{"chunk_id":"9d21b8","wall_time_seconds":1.9321565,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":2893,"output":"---\\r\\ntitle: Teaching Voice\\r\\ntype: concept\\r\\ntags: [lsat-u, voice, pedagogy, content]\\r\\ncreated: 2026-06-10\\r\\nupdated: 2026-07-18\\r\\nstatus: active\\r\\nsubject: Teaching Voice\\r\\naliases: []\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n# Teaching Voice\\r\\n\\r\\nHow LSAT U sounds, across every surface. This is the canonical voice doc: route all student-facing and brand copy through it. Built from a grill with Joshua (2026-06-13), then tested and enriched against the full corpus of his real correspondence (944 messages he authored, mid-2025 to mid-2026, from the Gmail takeout; 2026-07-18). Claims below marked with a quote are evidenced by that corpus.\\r\\n\\r\\nIt replaces the old two-register / 15-named-tools \\"preserve verbatim\\" profile (deleted 2026-06-10) and folds in the brand/marketing register the earlier draft was missing.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Core voice (every register)\\r\\n\\r\\nThe constant under all three registers below. This is Joshua on the page.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Quiet authority.** State the value and let it land. Never oversell, never beg, never perform enthusiasm.\\r\\n- **Specific, never generic.** Real scores, the actual skill, the student\'s own history. Praise is a specific observation, not \\"great job.\\"\\r\\n- **Honest about the work, gentle about the person.** Be blunt that the LSAT is hard (\\"expect this to be exhausting and very challenging\\"). Never be blunt about a student\'s shortcomings. Honesty points at the material; warmth points at the person. When someone slips, nudge gently, never accuse.\\r\\n- **Light, grounded metaphor, understated in email.** In his real correspondence the recurring image is quiet: \\"partner with you on your LSAT journey,\\" \\"getting set up,\\" \\"foundational.\\" The vivid images (runway, climb, march toward November, an easy door to walk through) belong to authored teaching and brand copy, not to email. Keep metaphor light and grounded; never float off into abstraction.\\r\\n- **Balanced rhythm.** Short declaratives plus one slightly longer warm beat. Air between ideas. Each idea gets its own line. Real messages are short and single-purpose (median ~280 characters).\\r\\n- **Plain professional diction.** No corporate jargon, no startup hype (\\"unlock,\\" \\"crush,\\" \\"level up,\\" \\"game-changer\\" — \\"crush\\" appears once in 944 messages). Contractions are the norm, not the exception. Exclamation points are genuine, not performed: a warm message often carries one, occasionally more, especially in openers (\\"Sorry for such a long delay!\\"). He is not exclamation-averse.\\r\\n- **Forward-looking.** End on the next step or what\'s ahead.\\r\\n- **No em dashes, ever.** Use periods, colons before lists, the middot (·) as a separator, and numbered steps for procedures.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Openings, closings, and signature phrases\\r\\n\\r\\nThe mechanical fingerprint of his email, from the real corpus. Match these when drafting as Joshua.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Greeting.** \\"Hi [Name],\\" is the default (used ~519x). \\"Hey [Name],\\" for established/returning students (~229x, warmer). \\"Hello [Name],\\" (~105x) and \\"Dear [Name],\\" (~18x, formal) for first contact or a more formal note.\\r\\n- **Sign-off.** \\"Best,\\" and \\"Best regards,\\" are the workhorses (~360x / ~237x). \\"Thanks,\\" when it\'s a favor or logistics (~146x). \\"Warmly,\\" / \\"Warm regards,\\" (~54x) for a genuinely warm note. \\"Talk soon,\\" (~9x) for someone he\'ll see again soon.\\r\\n- **Signature.** Almost always signed **\\"Joshua\\"** (844 of 944 messages). The name is near-universal; include it.\\r\\n- **Signature phrases (his verbal fingerprint, use naturally, don\'t overuse):** \\"let me know\\" (by far the most common, ~390x), \\"looking forward,\\" \\"I hope\\" / \\"hope all is well\\" / \\"hope you,\\" \\"no worries at all,\\" \\"happy to\\" / \\"more than happy to,\\" \\"just wanted to make sure,\\" \\"make sure,\\" \\"no rush,\\" \\"of course.\\"\\r\\n- **Punctuation he actually uses:** semicolons (correctly, ~41x); ellipses essentially never. (For em-dashes, the hard rule in Core voice governs — never.)\\r\\n\\r\\n## The apology / accountability move\\r\\n\\r\\nOne of his most frequent and characteristic behaviors, and worth naming on its own. When he is late to reply, or missed or mishandled something, he opens by owning it plainly, often with a brief honest reason, then pivots straight to the fix. No over-apologizing, no excuses dressed up.\\r\\n\\r\\n> I\'m so sorry. I thought I had let you know ... I clearly didn\'t communicate that as well as I should have.\\r\\n\\r\\n> I\'ve been away from work for personal reasons, but I\'m back now and getting caught up.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe pattern: own it in the first line, give the real reason in one clause, move to what happens next. Warm, candid, brief.\\r\\n\\r\\n## When something on his side broke (approved shape, 2026-09-11)\\r\\n\\r\\nFrom the Sandra booking-error reply, edited by Joshua line by line over three drafts and then sent as-is. Use this shape whenever a student hit a bug or a mistake that was his. The sent text is the reference:\\r\\n\\r\\n> Hi Sandra,\\r\\n>\\r\\n> I\'m sorry about this. The error was on my end, not yours.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> To confirm: none of your bookings went through, so nothing is on the calendar yet. The page was showing a few times that the system then refused, and it looks like you landed on those. That is fixed now.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Your link is the same one as before:\\r\\n> [link]\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Pick any time it shows and it will book. If it\'s easier, just send me the time you were trying for and I\'ll add it to the schedule myself.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> If you run into any other issues, let me know.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Once again, my apologies.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Best,\\r\\n> Joshua\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Apology first, as the opening line.** \\"I\'m sorry about this. The error was on my end, not yours.\\" The ownership sits in the first two sentences, before any explanation.\\r\\n2. **State their position plainly, as a confirmation.** \\"To confirm: none of your bookings went through, so nothing is on the calendar yet.\\" Answer the question they actually asked. Don\'t mention the package or credits unless the situation calls for it.\\r\\n3. **One-sentence explanation, then \\"That is fixed now.\\"** No mechanics, no system names.\\r\\n4. **Hand them the next step, plus the manual fallback.** The link, \\"pick any time it shows and it will book,\\" and the offer to do it by hand: \\"If it\'s easier, just send me the time you were trying for and I\'ll add it to the schedule myself.\\"\\r\\n5. **Invite the next report:** \\"If you run into any other issues, let me know.\\"\\r\\n6. **Close with \\"Once again, my apologies.\\"** then \\"Best,\\" and \\"Joshua\\".\\r\\n\\r\\nCut from the draft, do not reuse:\\r\\n- \\"Sorry for the runaround\\" as a sign-off. The apology opens the email; it is not a closing quip.\\r\\n- \\"You will get a calendar invite with the Google Meet link right after.\\" Do not narrate what the system will send; it reads as a promise about machinery.\\r\\n- \\"You have all 10 sessions\\" / \\"nothing was used from your package.\\" Leave the package out unless it is needed; the reassurance they want is that nothing is booked, not an accounting.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Situational micro-templates\\r\\n\\r\\nVerbatim-grounded reference lines for the situations that recur most. Adapt, never paste blindly.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Student reschedules / cancels:** low-pressure, no guilt.\\r\\n  > No worries at all. It happens, so please don\'t worry about it. If you would like to reschedule, just let me know.\\r\\n- **He missed / no-showed (approved make-good template):** full ownership, real reason, offer to make it right (see the apology move above). When the cause was an unexpected health issue, the approved shape is: sincerely apologize, state that a serious health scare unexpectedly took him out of commission, offer a **completely free, full LSAT session**, and hand them the complimentary booking link `https://cal.com/joshua-jtx5ud/complimentary-session`. Emphasis stays limited: bold the complimentary offer, italicize the line that one focused session can put points on the board. Draft in Gmail; never send without Joshua\'s explicit go-ahead.\\r\\n- **Consultation reminder (day-of):**\\r\\n  > Just checking in before our consultation today. Looking forward to speaking with you. I just wanted to make sure everything is still good.\\r\\n- **Consultation follow-up:** warm, specific to their situation.\\r\\n  > Really nice meeting you. I enjoyed our conversation ... I\'m glad we got to talk through where you\'re at and what you\'re aiming for on test day.\\r\\n- **Inbound prospect (hasn\'t booked):** state availability plainly, no overselling, hand them the next step.\\r\\n  > Thanks for reaching out ... I\'d be happy to talk more about what you\'re working on and see if we\'d be a good fit. You can schedule a consultation here.\\r\\n- **Student under real-life stress:** meet the person first.\\r\\n  > Please don\'t apologize ... it sounds like you are dealing with an incredibly stressful and demanding situation.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The three registers\\r\\n\\r\\nWhich voice governs which surface.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 1. Coaching (earnest) -- inbox, recaps, in-drill feedback, email\\r\\n\\r\\nFully earnest. Warm, sincere, calm, patient. No jokes. The closest thing to being in the room with Joshua. Normalizes struggle, then moves to the work.\\r\\n\\r\\nReference line (target tone):\\r\\n\\r\\n> Totally normal to trip on this one. Let\'s slow down: what is the author actually concluding? Once you see it, the trap answers lose their grip. You\'ve got this.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Encouragement (student missed a hard one):** honest first, then forward. Name that it\'s genuinely hard, stay calm, move to the work. Not soft-reassuring, not cold.\\r\\n  > Missing this is expected. It\'s one of the hardest moves on the test. Let\'s slow down and see where it slipped.\\r\\n- **Accountability (student isn\'t doing the work):** gentle nudge, low pressure. Frame it as a slip, find a rhythm together. Never \\"the reps aren\'t happening,\\" never tough love.\\r\\n- **Praise (student nails it):** name the exact skill, tie it to their history, raise the bar.\\r\\n  > That\'s the cleanest you\'ve split premise from conclusion yet. Let\'s push it into the harder sets.\\r\\n- **Hard truth about the test:** state it plainly. \\"Do not expect for it to come easy. Expect to find this exhausting.\\"\\r\\n\\r\\n### 2. Teaching content (earnest substance, wit at the edges) -- bootcamp lessons, drill explanations\\r\\n\\r\\nThe substance stays earnest and clear (you are explaining a hard skill). The wit lives only at the edges: headers, openers, transitions. No jokes mid-explanation, nothing that costs comprehension.\\r\\n\\r\\n> Header: \\"The flaw hides in plain sight.\\"\\r\\n> Body: earnest, clear, step by step.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 3. Brand (sharp wit) -- landing, auth, marketing\\r\\n\\r\\nConfident and clever, the way a good lawyer is clever. Wit tied to the real skill, not wordplay for its own sake. Playful is allowed, but every clever line must be earned and true. Hollow cleverness fails (the killed \\"the next card is the page in front of you\\" was clever but empty).\\r\\n\\r\\n> Most prep teaches the test. We teach the tell.\\r\\n\\r\\nBrand copy speaks as the platform (\\"we\\", \\"you\\"), not as an individual (\\"I\\", \\"Joshua\\"). The product is the coach; no single person narrates the marketing.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Don\'t\\r\\n\\r\\n- No cold-testing or gotcha tone. (Ties to teach-first-calibrate-after.)\\r\\n- No condescension or empty cheerleading. Encouragement must sit on real substance.\\r\\n- No generic praise, no hollow cleverness, no hedging (\\"you might want to\\").\\r\\n- No hype/startup vocabulary.\\r\\n- No em dashes, ever.\\r\\n\\r\\nCorrections log: [[COPY-CORRECTIONS]] records every student-facing wording fix and\\r\\nthe reason it was wrong. Read it before writing or editing LSAT U copy.\\r\\n\\r\\nRelated: teach-first-calibrate-after, LSAT U. Source samples: `raw/templates/Golden Email Template Playbook.md`, `raw/templates/email_writing_examples_11_full.txt`, and the full authored-email corpus from the Gmail takeout (944 messages, analyzed 2026-07-18; takeout at `raw/sources/private/takeout/`, git-ignored).\\r\\n"}}}'}]

[{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 1.8 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"78f5ac","wall_time_seconds":1.5797523999999998,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":3570,"output":"# Copy corrections\\r\\n\\r\\nEvery student-facing wording fix, with the reason it was wrong. Read this before\\r\\nwriting or editing copy for LSAT U so the same mistake is not made twice.\\r\\n\\r\\nCompanion to [[teaching-voice]], which says how the writing should sound. This\\r\\nsays what has actually gone wrong and why.\\r\\n\\r\\nStarted 2026-09-07 from a Read, Recall, Colour pass. Add to it every time a\\r\\ncorrection is made.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The rules these corrections came from\\r\\n\\r\\nThree rules already existed and all three leaked anyway, because each was\\r\\nenforced on the components that happened to exist when it was written. A surface\\r\\nadded later starts uncovered.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **No em dashes, ever.** [[teaching-voice]], Core voice.\\r\\n- **No internal vocabulary in student copy.** `projects/lsatu/src/features/activity-centre/CONTEXT.md`\\r\\n  carries the glossary and marks what to avoid.\\r\\n- **Every CSS token a stylesheet uses must be defined in it.** `projects/lsatu/CLAUDE.md`.\\r\\n\\r\\nGuards now live with the content rather than with each component:\\r\\n`content/instructions-voice.test.ts` checks the authored instructions, so every\\r\\nsurface that renders them is covered, including surfaces not written yet.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Corrections\\r\\n\\r\\n### Generic reasoning prompts → concrete numbered demonstrations (2026-09-30)\\r\\n\\r\\nJoshua marked four parts of the V6 opening: \\"Read each whole idea,\\" \\"Find what the statements guarantee,\\" the abstract first sentence about information, and the paragraph combining application and linking. They named goals without showing a useful action or explanation. Replace them with numbered, separate scenarios. Show the fact and rule that prove a conclusion about one case; separately show two matching rules and their new conditional conclusion. Labels should identify actual inputs or outputs. Review the whole note for repeated umbrella instructions and make task instructions executable. This follows the teaching voice: specific, concrete, short sentences, with air between distinct ideas.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Fact and rule definitions must explain the inference (2026-09-30)\\r\\n\\r\\nJoshua rejected definitions that remained abstract and an explanation that did not clearly distinguish applying a rule from linking rules. Define the inputs with examples, then show the matching step and exact output. A case fact plus a rule proves something about that case. Two connecting rules produce another conditional rule without establishing a case exists. Adding a fact to the chain is a separate step. Explain all four fact situations and a hidden chain revealed by contraposition rather than leaving them implicit in an interactive model. Rules include general logical relationships, not only policies or obligations.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Boxed `L -> R` → bold teaching notation **L → R** (2026-09-30)\\r\\n\\r\\nJoshua rejected the recap\'s small monospace arrow inside a pale code box. It looked like implementation text and weakened the explanation. Use a real, clearly weighted arrow in ordinary teaching typography. Explain its complete conditions before shortening them. The Some, Most, and All reference also governs the progression: introduce the whole idea, develop the individual components, then compare and combine them. A visual refresh must review that sequence, not only colors and boxes.\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"Concept lesson\\" → the actual reasoning title (2026-09-30)\\r\\n\\r\\nThe recap preview exposed an internal label above the student lesson. Joshua explicitly rejected it. Use a title such as \\"Facts, Rules, and What Follows\\" and headings that teach the reasoning. Keep production labels, version metadata, and design commentary in private records. Check the rendered HTML, since its shell can introduce wording absent from the Markdown source.\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"Recall Rephrase Colour\\" → \\"Read, Recall, Colour\\"\\r\\nThe door\'s heading was hardcoded to a name the product does not have, one line\\r\\nunder a chip reading \\"Read, Recall, Colour\\". \\"Rephrase\\" belongs to a different\\r\\nActivity, Conditional Rephrase. A test asserted the wrong name, which is why\\r\\n2,600 passing tests never caught it.\\r\\n**Lesson:** when a test pins a string, check the string is right, not just that\\r\\nit matches.\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"Intake only. Nothing comes back out yet…\\" → plain instruction\\r\\nClinical and abstract, and the sentence then told her to read \\"with full\\r\\nintonation\\" while step one is silent reading. The clause that made intonation\\r\\ninternal, \\"hear it naturally in your head\\", had been dropped in an earlier edit.\\r\\n**Lesson:** a word like \\"intake\\" reads as jargon. And when copy is trimmed,\\r\\ncheck what the trimmed clause was load-bearing for.\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"Three beats through the stimulus\\" → \\"Three steps\\"\\r\\n\\"Beat\\" is the internal code name for one of the four method steps. The glossary\\r\\nsays students see **step**. The interface ten pixels below labelled the same four\\r\\nthings Step 1 to Step 4, so the page used two names for one thing.\\r\\n**Lesson:** never let an implementation name reach the page.\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"22 pieces to read\\" → line removed\\r\\nA **piece** is one chunk, roughly a sentence, and the instructions on that same\\r\\npage use the word that way. The count was of stimuli, so \\"22 pieces\\" read as 22\\r\\nsentences.\\r\\n**Lesson:** a unit word must mean one thing per surface. Check what a word\\r\\nalready means on the page before reusing it.\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"say it back\\" → \\"tell it back\\", \\"The Read\\" → \\"The Recall\\"\\r\\nThe library door still carried both retired names. \\"The Read\\" was step four\'s\\r\\nformer name and collided with step one, which is why it was renamed.\\r\\n**Lesson:** a rename is not finished until every row carries it. The door was\\r\\nstale for months because it is a different database row from the sections.\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"then a fourth\\" → \\"then a fourth step\\"\\r\\nThe noun sat three words back and the reader had to carry it.\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"once you have got all of it\\" → \\"once you have read all of it\\"\\r\\nAmbiguous between having read it and having remembered it, in the one clause\\r\\nthat triggers step four.\\r\\n**Lesson:** precision matters most where the sentence is an instruction.\\r\\n\\r\\n### The three-fact notice → one fact\\r\\n\\"Nothing is recording yet, the microphone opens on Start, and the section\\r\\nrecords in one take that you cannot pause.\\" Two of those are said again in step\\r\\nfour and in the long version, so she skipped the paragraph.\\r\\n**Lesson:** say it once, in the place it matters.\\r\\n\\r\\n### The method, told twice → the long version collapsed\\r\\nThe page rendered four numbered steps and then the whole written briefing saying\\r\\nthe same thing at length, both open. She read the method twice and could not\\r\\ntell which one to follow.\\r\\n**Lesson:** two explanations of one thing is worse than either alone.\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"PT105.S1 · 24 stimuli · about 25 min\\" → removed\\r\\nThe section was already the second line of the title. The clock is at the foot\\r\\nand in the long version. The stimulus count measured the work in a unit she has\\r\\nno feel for.\\r\\n**Lesson:** delete a line that repeats what is above it. Do not reword it.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Booking emails: hand over the link, not the pass settings (2026-09-08)\\r\\n\\r\\n**Cut:** \\"70 minutes each, and no expiration date, so there\'s no rush to use them.\\"\\r\\n**Keep:** \\"You\'re set up on LSAT U with 10 sessions.\\"\\r\\n\\r\\nSession length and expiry are admin fields. The student sees them on the booking\\r\\npage when she picks a time, so putting them in the email is detail she did not ask\\r\\nfor and has to read past to reach the link. The credit count is worth saying because\\r\\nit tells her how much she has. Everything else about the pass stays in the backend.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Lesson:** in a booking email, say who it\'s for, how many sessions, and the link.\\r\\nStop there.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Drill hub: say what the button does, not what the feature is called (2026-09-09)\\r\\n\\r\\nSix changes on `/classroom/drill`, from the run-3 pass. The hub named its own\\r\\nfeatures, and it assumed the student had rejected something.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Was | Now |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| \\"Start Smart Drill\\" | \\"Practice your weakest types\\" |\\r\\n| \\"Start One Passage\\" | \\"Read one passage\\" |\\r\\n| \\"Start a Smart Drill instead\\" | \\"Or practice your weakest types\\" |\\r\\n| \\"Read one passage instead\\" | \\"Or read one passage now\\" |\\r\\n| \\"Open analytics\\" | \\"See where you lose points\\" |\\r\\n| \\"Open journal\\" | \\"Review your missed questions\\" |\\r\\n\\r\\n\\"Smart Drill\\" is the product\'s internal name for the adaptive set. On a button it\\r\\nasks the student to guess what she is about to get. The sentence above the button\\r\\nstill names it, which is where a product name belongs: after the thing has been\\r\\nexplained, not as the explanation.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\"Instead\\" was the worse one. It tells the student she has just declined the\\r\\nassigned work by reading past it. She has not. \\"Or\\" offers a second path without\\r\\nnarrating a decision she never made.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\"Open analytics\\" and \\"Open journal\\" name a screen. A student does not want\\r\\nanalytics, she wants to know where the points are going.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe fallback paragraph lost \\"an adaptive set that follows your weakest question\\r\\ntypes\\" for \\"the question types you miss most\\": the same fact, without the product\\r\\nvocabulary.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Lesson:** a button says what happens next, in the student\'s words. Feature names\\r\\nbelong in the sentence that explains them, never on the control.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Words never to use in student copy\\r\\n\\r\\nFrom the glossary. Internal names may stay in code, never on the page.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Never | Use instead |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| beat, beats | step |\\r\\n| chunk | piece |\\r\\n| intake | plain instruction |\\r\\n| briefing, phase, tab, card | the thing\'s own name |\\r\\n| say it back | tell it back |\\r\\n| The Read | The Recall |\\r\\n| Recall Rephrase Colour | Read, Recall, Colour |\\r\\n| em dash, en dash | a full stop, or a colon before a list |\\r\\n\\r\\n## Conditional Rephrase: name the student action, not the internal model (2026-09-15)\\r\\n\\r\\n**Cut:** “record the route,” “choose the route,” and a map presented as five rules.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Keep:** diagram the statement on paper, choose the matching diagram, and organize\\r\\nthe map into four groups. “Required means right” is a separate takeaway because it\\r\\nexplains placement; it is not a fifth group.\\r\\n\\r\\n“Route” described the system’s representation, not the student’s work. Calling five\\r\\nunlike ideas rules also flattened the teaching structure and made the layout harder to\\r\\nread.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Lesson:** name the action the student can see herself doing. Do not force a teaching\\r\\nreminder into the same hierarchy as the categories it explains.\\r\\n\\r\\nRelated: [[teaching-voice]] · [[ASSIGN-AN-ACTIVITY]] · [[STUDENT-PLATFORM-IDENTITY-MAP]]\\r\\n\\r\\n## Session recaps: write a reusable reference, not a play-by-play (2026-09-12)\\r\\n\\r\\n**Cut:** an opener saying the student got two questions right, followed by a summary of\\r\\nwhich answer they chose and how they explained it.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Keep:** the concept the student needs tomorrow, a visual model of the reasoning, a\\r\\nshort diagnostic check, and the exact practice they need to complete.\\r\\n\\r\\nA student will not remember an isolated answer-choice exchange a day later, and the\\r\\nexchange is not useful unless it demonstrates a reusable rule. A recap should read like\\r\\na compact study note, not a record of the conversation. Name a question only when the\\r\\ndetails make the concept easier to apply. Praise belongs only when it identifies a\\r\\ndurable skill or meaningful change, not merely that an answer was correct.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Lesson:** organize the recap around what the student can use next. Lead with the\\r\\nconcept, show the logic clearly, and finish with tangible practice.\\r\\n\\r\\n### A rule is not a fact (2026-09-12)\\r\\n\\r\\n**Cut:** describing a conditional Must Be True lesson as “applying a rule to a fact”\\r\\nwithout checking whether the stimulus supplied a fact at all.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Keep:** a fact is an asserted true case or condition. A rule is a general conditional\\r\\nrelationship. It tells you what follows if its trigger is present, but it does not say\\r\\nthat the trigger occurred. Some stimuli contain rules only, so the work is to chain\\r\\nthem. When a fact is present, apply a matching rule or a valid contrapositive.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Lesson:** label the role of each sentence before explaining the inference. text(await tools.apply_patch("*** Begin Patch\n*** Add File: C:\\Users\\Joshu\\dev\\ai-os\\brainstorms\\2026-09-30-conditional-curriculum\\group-1-learning-and-drills.md\n+# Group 1: identify what guarantees what\n+\n+Draft: 2026-10-01. Original LSAT U teaching and exercises for Joshua's review. This file does not publish, assign or change platform content.\n+\n+## Give the teacher two independently assignable choices\n+\n+1. **Learn and practice Group 1:** the explanation, worked examples, guided attempts, selected existing practice and fresh independent practice below.\n+2. **Practice Group 1:** the standalone drills below, with the teaching available as a reference. Beginner, Medium and Advanced are separate sets within the drill.\n+\n+Existing Activities remain reusable. These eighteen fresh items supplement them rather than replace their content. Difficulty describes interpretation and reasoning demand. Beginner is untimed. Timing may be offered for Medium and Advanced after accurate untimed work; no time limit is specified or approved here.\n+\n+**Hint behavior is proposed, pending Joshua's reply:** each item has one optional, specific hint requested by the student. Keep it separate from the answer. Record whether it was used so a supported response is distinguishable from an independent one. This draft does not prescribe scoring penalties, advancement percentages or automatic mastery thresholds.\n+\n+## A guarantee gives you a direction\n+\n+If a storage unit's alarm is armed, its status light is illuminated.\n+\n+The sufficient condition is **the storage unit's alarm is armed**. That is enough to guarantee **its status light is illuminated**, the necessary condition.\n+\n+**Alarm armed → status light illuminated.**\n+\n+The rule does not say that an alarm is armed now. It tells you what follows if an alarm is armed. A separate fact, such as “Unit 12's alarm is armed,” lets you apply the rule to Unit 12. You can then conclude that Unit 12's status light is illuminated.\n+\n+An illuminated light does not prove an armed alarm. The light could be illuminated in another way. An unarmed alarm does not prove an unilluminated light either. The rule gives no outcome for that starting situation. Both conclusions would add a direction the author did not give you.\n+\n+For the rule **alarm armed → light illuminated**, compare these fully described cases:\n+\n+| Case | Does it fit the rule? | Why |\n+|---|---|---|\n+| Alarm armed; light illuminated | Allowed | The stated guarantee is satisfied. |\n+| Alarm armed; light not illuminated | Forbidden | The sufficient condition occurs without its required result. |\n+| Alarm not armed; light illuminated | Allowed | The rule does not prohibit other ways to illuminate the light. |\n+| Alarm not armed; light not illuminated | Allowed | The rule makes no positive demand when its trigger is absent. |\n+\n+“Allowed” means consistent with the rule. It does not mean the case actually happened. When judging a conclusion from supplied information, use **Guaranteed**, **Ruled out** or **Unknown**. Unknown means the conclusion could be true or false while the supplied information stays true. This avoids treating “possible” as “proven.”\n+\n+## Translate complete ideas before shortening them\n+\n+Use these four steps:\n+\n+1. Identify the phrase expressing the guarantee.\n+2. Write the complete condition that is sufficient. Include its subject, action, negatives and relevant modifiers.\n+3. Write the complete condition that follows. Keep the same person or object when the sentence concerns one subject.\n+4. Write **sufficient condition → necessary condition**, then read it as an ordinary if-then sentence. Compare that sentence with the original.\n+\n+Short labels come after those complete ideas. For example, “a delivery vehicle is registered with the harbor office” may become **registered with harbor office**. It should not become just **vehicle**, because that loses the condition you need to satisfy.\n+\n+### Worked example: a universal statement has the same direction\n+\n+Every delivery vehicle registered with the harbor office displays a numbered permit.\n+\n+The sufficient condition is **a delivery vehicle is registered with the harbor office**. The necessary condition is **that vehicle displays a numbered permit**.\n+\n+**Delivery vehicle registered with harbor office → displays numbered permit.**\n+\n+Read it back: if a delivery vehicle is registered with the harbor office, that vehicle displays a numbered permit. The complete subject survives. The statement does not say that every delivery vehicle displays a permit. It also does not say that every vehicle displaying a permit is registered with that office.\n+\n+### Guided attempt: clause order does not decide direction\n+\n+A status report is sent whenever a sensor restarts.\n+\n+1. Which complete idea follows whenever?\n+2. What does the statement guarantee from that idea?\n+3. Write the arrow and read it back in English.\n+\n+**Optional hint:** the sufficient condition can appear second in the sentence. Start with the idea introduced by whenever.\n+\n+**Answer:** **Sensor restarts → status report sent.** Whenever the sensor restarts, a report is sent. A sent report alone does not establish that the sensor restarted.\n+\n+### Guided attempt: keep a modifier inside the subject\n+\n+Any membership application submitted through the evening service receives a confirmation number.\n+\n+1. Is the subject every application, or a restricted group of applications?\n+2. Write that complete sufficient condition.\n+3. State what follows about that same application.\n+\n+**Optional hint:** include how the application was submitted before putting it left of the arrow.\n+\n+**Answer:** **Membership application submitted through evening service → receives confirmation number.** The rule gives no guarantee for an application submitted through another service.\n+\n+## Read the sentence before trusting an indicator list\n+\n+Group 1 commonly includes if, whenever, when, where, every, all, any and the only. Guarantee verbs can express the same direction. A list helps you recognize familiar wording; the sentence determines whether a guarantee is present and what its conditions are.\n+\n+- **When** can report a single event: “When I arrived on Tuesday, the lights were off.” That sentence does not establish a general arrival-to-darkness rule.\n+- **Where** can identify a location rather than a guarantee. Ask what the sentence actually commits the author to.\n+- **If** can appear in an indirect question: “We asked if the certificate was valid.” That does not give a conditional rule.\n+- **The only** needs careful parsing. “The only applications accepted are applications with a signed declaration” gives **application accepted → has signed declaration**. It does not make a declaration sufficient for acceptance. Do not assign a direction merely to the next isolated noun.\n+\n+Group 2 develops requirement language such as only if and requires. Groups 3 and 4 develop translation that changes a condition's negation. This Group 1 package can compare directions, but it does not claim to teach those groups' procedures. Negatives already written inside a Group 1 condition must still be preserved.\n+\n+## Use harder Group 1 language after its prerequisites\n+\n+Medium adds longer predicates, clause placement, simple existing negation and contextual indicator checks. It does not require contraposition, compound connective rules or chains.\n+\n+Advanced returns to sufficient-condition language with explicit dependencies:\n+\n+- **A1:** joint AND antecedents. Teach first that both conditions are required together; one alone cannot trigger the rule.\n+- **A2:** inclusive OR antecedents. Teach first that either branch can satisfy that antecedent; both are also permitted unless the statement excludes them.\n+- **A3:** complete modifier scope. No AND/OR notation or contraposition required if the whole restricted subject remains one predicate.\n+- **A4:** contraposition. Teach first that failure of the necessary condition excludes the sufficient condition. Keep the person and complete predicates consistent.\n+- **A5:** rule versus existence. Teach first that a universal rule does not establish that any qualifying case exists.\n+- **A6:** direct chaining and fact application. Teach first that a rule's result must satisfy the next rule's trigger. Linking rules alone does not establish a case; the supplied fact activates the chain here.\n+\n+Assign these items only after the named dependency has been taught. They are harder applications of Group 1 language, not a substitute for those lessons.\n+\n+## Beginner: six independent attempts\n+\n+### B1. Build the rule from every\n+\n+**Task:** Every inventory tag printed in orange is included in the daily inspection list. Write the complete sufficient and necessary conditions, then diagram the rule.\n+\n+**Answer:** **Inventory tag printed in orange → included in daily inspection list.**\n+\n+**Explanation:** The guarantee applies to tags printed in orange. It does not apply to every inventory tag, and it does not tell you the color of other listed tags.\n+\n+**Optional hint:** include “printed in orange” in the left condition.\n+\n+### B2. Build the rule when if comes second\n+\n+**Task:** A parcel is released from the archive if its pickup receipt is signed. Diagram the rule without changing either predicate.\n+\n+**Answer:** **Parcel's pickup receipt signed → parcel released from archive.**\n+\n+**Explanation:** The if-clause identifies what is sufficient, even though it comes second. Release is the guaranteed result.\n+\n+**Optional hint:** begin with the receipt condition, not the first clause on the page.\n+\n+### B3. Classify complete cases\n+\n+**Task:** If an access code is accepted, the green light is on. Mark each case Allowed or Forbidden: (a) accepted code, green light on; (b) accepted code, green light off; (c) code not accepted, green light on; (d) code not accepted, green light off.\n+\n+**Answer:** (a) Allowed; (b) Forbidden; (c) Allowed; (d) Allowed.\n+\n+**Explanation:** Only (b) supplies the sufficient condition while denying its required result. The rule gives no required outcome when a code is not accepted. Allowed cases are possible, not necessarily actual.\n+\n+**Optional hint:** find the case where the trigger occurs but its result does not.\n+\n+### B4. Separate a result from proof of its trigger\n+\n+**Task:** Every document entered in the tracking register receives a reference number. Document R has received a reference number. Is “Document R was entered in the tracking register” Guaranteed, Ruled out or Unknown?\n+\n+**Answer:** Unknown.\n+\n+**Explanation:** Entry guarantees a number. Having a number does not establish entry. Document R could have received its number through another process, or through this one.\n+\n+**Optional hint:** compare the supplied fact with the right side of your arrow.\n+\n+### B5. Repair an inference from an absent trigger\n+\n+**Task:** If a volunteer attends the briefing, the volunteer receives a printed guide. Neri did not attend the briefing. A student concludes, “Neri did not receive a printed guide.” Repair the student's conclusion.\n+\n+**Answer:** Whether Neri received a printed guide is Unknown.\n+\n+**Explanation:** Attendance is one sufficient way to receive a guide. The rule does not prohibit giving a guide to someone who did not attend. Negating the sufficient condition does not establish a negated result.\n+\n+**Optional hint:** does the rule say attendance is the only way to receive a guide?\n+\n+### B6. Apply the rule to its matching fact\n+\n+**Task:** Any subscriber whose account is active receives the weekly digest. Bela is a subscriber whose account is active. State the guaranteed conclusion about Bela and identify why it follows.\n+\n+**Answer:** Bela receives the weekly digest.\n+\n+**Explanation:** Bela satisfies the complete sufficient condition: subscriber with an active account. Apply the guarantee to that same person. The rule by itself would not establish that Bela's account is active; the separate fact does.\n+\n+**Optional hint:** match Bela's fact to the entire subject described by any.\n+\n+## Medium: six attempts with more demanding language\n+\n+### M1. Preserve the restricted subject\n+\n+**Task:** Every research report using confidential survey data undergoes an ethics review. Report S uses public survey data; it uses no confidential survey data. Is “Report S undergoes an ethics review” Guaranteed, Ruled out or Unknown? Write the rule before answering.\n+\n+**Answer:** **Research report using confidential survey data → undergoes ethics review.** The conclusion is Unknown.\n+\n+**Explanation:** Report S does not satisfy this trigger. That fails to prove a review, but it also fails to rule a review out. Another policy could require one.\n+\n+**Optional hint:** do not shorten the left side to “research report.”\n+\n+### M2. Interpret the only as a complete sentence\n+\n+**Task:** The only records accepted by the licensing office are digitally signed records. Diagram the relationship. Does a digital signature alone prove acceptance?\n+\n+**Answer:** **Record accepted by licensing office → digitally signed.** A digital signature alone does not prove acceptance.\n+\n+**Explanation:** The sentence restricts the accepted records to digitally signed records. It does not say every signed record is accepted.\n+\n+**Optional hint:** start with a record that the office has accepted. What must be true of it?\n+\n+### M3. Keep timing inside the predicate\n+\n+**Task:** A backup log is opened before 05:00 whenever that day's scheduled backup starts after midnight. Diagram the rule. A scheduled backup starts at 23:00. Does the rule guarantee that its log will not be opened before 05:00?\n+\n+**Answer:** **That day's scheduled backup starts after midnight → its log opened before 05:00.** No; the proposed negative conclusion is unsupported.\n+\n+**Explanation:** The rule guarantees an early log opening for the stated start-time condition. A 23:00 start does not satisfy that condition, but it does not prohibit an early log opening. Assume times refer to the relevant backup's stated schedule, with no additional timing policy supplied.\n+\n+**Optional hint:** first preserve both time phrases; then check whether the fact satisfies the stated trigger.\n+\n+### M4. Preserve a negative already in the trigger\n+\n+**Task:** If a permit has not expired, its holder may enter the exhibit. The permit held by Ivo has not expired. What follows? Does the rule also tell you what follows for an expired permit?\n+\n+**Answer:** Ivo may enter the exhibit. For an expired permit, permission to enter is Unknown from this rule alone.\n+\n+**Explanation:** The complete sufficient condition includes not expired. Ivo meets it. An expired permit negates that trigger, which does not prove lack of permission. “May enter” means permission, not proof of actual entry.\n+\n+**Optional hint:** distinguish permission to enter from the act of entering.\n+\n+### M5. Repair the direction of a guarantee verb\n+\n+**Task:** The policy says that completing the identity check guarantees issuance of a visitor pass. A student diagrams **Visitor pass issued → identity check completed**. Repair the diagram and explain why the first version added information.\n+\n+**Answer:** **Identity check completed → visitor pass issued.**\n+\n+**Explanation:** Completing the check is sufficient for issuance. The reversed arrow would claim that every issued pass proves a completed check, excluding other possible ways to obtain a pass that this policy does not exclude.\n+\n+**Optional hint:** ask which event the policy says is enough for the other event.\n+\n+### M6. Distinguish a past event from a general guarantee\n+\n+**Task:** (a) When I visited the records room on Monday, its service window was closed. (b) Whenever the records room's alarm is being tested, its service window is closed. Which sentence supplies a general conditional rule? Diagram that rule. Does it connect visits with closures?\n+\n+**Answer:** Sentence (b): **Records room's alarm being tested → its service window closed.** It does not connect visits with closures.\n+\n+**Explanation:** Sentence (a) reports what happened during one visit. Sentence (b) guarantees closure under the stated testing condition. The occurrence of when in a sentence does not automatically establish a universal rule.\n+\n+**Optional hint:** look for a commitment about every qualifying occasion, rather than one dated occasion.\n+\n+## Advanced: six attempts after the named prerequisites\n+\n+### A1. Retain a joint trigger\n+\n+**Prerequisite:** AND antecedents.\n+\n+**Task:** If a proposal is filed before noon and carries the supervisor's signature, it enters today's review queue. Proposal T was filed before noon. Is “Proposal T enters today's review queue” Guaranteed, Ruled out or Unknown? Explain which condition is missing from the supplied facts.\n+\n+**Answer:** Unknown. Whether Proposal T carries the supervisor's signature is not supplied.\n+\n+**Explanation:** **Filed before noon AND carries supervisor's signature → enters today's queue.** The fact establishes only one part of the joint trigger. It does not establish the guarantee's prerequisites together. This also does not rule out queue entry through another rule.\n+\n+**Optional hint:** underline both conditions inside the if-clause before matching the fact.\n+\n+### A2. Use either sufficient branch without adding exclusivity\n+\n+**Prerequisite:** inclusive OR antecedents.\n+\n+**Task:** Any consignment arriving by rail or by ferry receives a transit code. Consignment U arrives by ferry. State what is guaranteed. Does the rule prohibit U from also arriving by rail as part of its journey?\n+\n+**Answer:** U receives a transit code. The rule does not prohibit it from also arriving by rail.\n+\n+**Explanation:** **Arrives by rail OR arrives by ferry → receives transit code.** The ferry branch satisfies the sufficient condition. Inclusive or allows either branch or both; the sentence gives no exclusivity requirement.\n+\n+**Optional hint:** one stated alternative can satisfy an inclusive-or trigger. Do not add “but not both.”\n+\n+### A3. Keep two modifiers attached to the same object\n+\n+**Prerequisite:** complete modifier scope; no compound notation required.\n+\n+**Task:** Every report released outside the agency without redactions receives a public-disclosure audit. Report V is released outside the agency, but it contains redactions. A student shortens the rule to **Released outside agency → receives audit**. Repair the shortened condition and judge whether V's audit is guaranteed.\n+\n+**Answer:** **Report released outside agency without redactions → receives public-disclosure audit.** An audit of V is not guaranteed; its audit status is Unknown.\n+\n+**Explanation:** The sufficient description contains both modifiers. V does not satisfy the complete description because it contains redactions. The shortened rule wrongly applies to a larger group of reports. The original still permits V to receive an audit for another reason.\n+\n+**Optional hint:** keep “without redactions” inside the description of the reports covered. Here it modifies the report's release, rather than supplying a separate Group 3 sentence to translate.\n+\n+### A4. Apply a contrapositive to complete predicates\n+\n+**Prerequisite:** contraposition.\n+\n+**Task:** Every technician certified for the pressure chamber has completed the current safety course. Mako has not completed the current safety course. What follows about Mako? State the original rule before using its contrapositive.\n+\n+**Answer:** **Technician certified for pressure chamber → completed current safety course.** Mako is not a technician certified for the pressure chamber.\n+\n+**Explanation:** **Not completed current safety course → not a technician certified for pressure chamber.** The fact denies the necessary condition and excludes the complete sufficient condition. It does not prove that Mako is not a technician at all or has never completed a different safety course.\n+\n+**Optional hint:** negate the entire certification description, not just the word technician.\n+\n+### A5. Avoid inventing an existing case\n+\n+**Prerequisite:** rule versus existence.\n+\n+**Task:** All permits issued by the coastal office this morning bear a blue seal. No other information is supplied. Which conclusion is guaranteed: (a) at least one blue-sealed permit exists; (b) if a permit was issued by that office this morning, it bears a blue seal; (c) every blue-sealed permit was issued by that office this morning?\n+\n+**Answer:** Only (b).\n+\n+**Explanation:** The rule gives **Permit issued by coastal office this morning → bears blue seal**. It does not establish that any permit was issued, so it does not prove (a). It also does not reverse the implication, so it does not prove (c).\n+\n+**Optional hint:** distinguish a rule describing qualifying permits from a fact that a qualifying permit exists.\n+\n+### A6. Transfer Group 1 translation into a short argument\n+\n+**Prerequisite:** direct chaining and fact application.\n+\n+**Task:** Everyone who completes the archive orientation is assigned a reader badge. Every person assigned a reader badge receives a locker code. Sol has completed the archive orientation. A student concludes that Sol receives a locker code and that everyone receiving a locker code has completed the orientation. Evaluate the two conclusions separately.\n+\n+**Answer:** Sol receives a locker code is Guaranteed. The universal claim about everyone receiving a locker code is not established.\n+\n+**Explanation:** **Completes archive orientation → assigned reader badge → receives locker code.** Sol's fact activates that chain. The second conclusion reverses the linked rule. The premises do not exclude other ways to receive a locker code.\n+\n+**Optional hint:** trace Sol forward from the supplied fact, then check whether the second conclusion tries to travel backward.\n+\n+## Reuse current content where it already does the job\n+\n+Local evidence comes from `C:/Users/Joshu/dev/lsatu-connected-experience`; this draft does not freshly verify the live site.\n+\n+| Existing asset | Reuse in this package | Boundary |\n+|---|---|---|\n+| `src/features/conditional-refresher/content.ts`, GROUPS g1 and DIAGRAM_ITEMS d1–d4 | Group 1 reference and simple diagram practice; reserve d4 until AND antecedents are taught | Four-group queues currently mix groups. No Group 1-only assignment is established. |\n+| Same content, FLASHCARDS f1/f8 and contrast f9; `ConditionalIndicatorsRefresher.tsx` | Paper diagram, ordinary-English retranslation, answer comparison and optional review | Self-ratings and browser-local totals are not independent teacher-visible mastery evidence. |\n+| `src/features/activity-centre/content/conditional-rephrase.json`, orders 1/3/5–9 | Existing sufficient-indicator practice after instruction | Select by actual predicate and demand; current General is a broad mixed assignment. |\n+| Same bank, orders 38/40/41/43/57 and part of 62 | Later look-alike, guarantee-language, compound and linking review after appropriate teaching | Review contextual wording before inclusion; a category label is not sufficient validation. |\n+| `src/features/activity-centre/components/PaperDiagramPanel.tsx` | Existing paper-first diagram/contrapositive comparison | Do not force contraposition into the first Beginner attempts before it is taught. |\n+| `src/features/activity-centre/worlds/switchyard/wings/SortingYard.tsx` and `rounds.ts` | Reuse the existing clause-placement interaction for guided direction practice | Component existence does not prove a currently assignable targeted exercise. |\n+| `src/lib/assignWork.ts` | Whole Activity or bootcamp assignment mechanisms | Separate Group 1 learning and standalone practice identities need packaging; no current skill-subset parameter was verified. |\n+\n+## Review what the student's response actually shows\n+\n+Check whether the student preserved the complete sufficient predicate, preserved its result, pointed the arrow correctly, matched a fact only when it satisfies the whole trigger, and distinguished a guaranteed conclusion from an allowed possibility. Do not regenerate at runtime.\\r\\n */\\r\\n\\r\\nexport interface PracticePool {\\r\\n  slug: string;\\r\\n  title: string;\\r\\n  /**\\r\\n   * Module-progress completion id written to completed_drills when this\\r\\n   * practice set is finished.
