The\\r\\n                answer choices test whether you understood the stimulus.\\r\\n              </p>\\r\\n            </div>\\r\\n          </CalloutCard>\\r\\n        </LessonSection>\\r\\n\\r\\n        <LessonSection tocTitle=\\"The Anatomy of a Logical Reasoning Question\\" className=\\"space-y-8 border-b-0\\">\\r\\n          <SectionHeading title=\\"Structure Example\\" subtitle=\\"The Anatomy of a Logical Reasoning Question\\" />\\r\\n          <p className=\\"text-[18px] leading-[1.7] text-[rgba(26,26,26,0.82)]\\">\\r\\n            This is one normal LR question. Touch the visible parts in order, then run the structure view on the\\r\\n            stimulus itself.\\r\\n          </p>\\r\\n          <QuestionAnatomyScanner />\\r\\n          <CalloutCard className=\\"bg-white\\" prominent>\\r\\n            <div className=\\"space-y-3 text-[18px] leading-[1.7] text-[rgba(26,26,26,0.82)]\\">\\r\\n              <p><strong>Stimulus:</strong> The stimulus is the content you are being asked about.</p>\\r\\n              <p><strong>Question Stem:</strong> The Question stem tells you the task.</p>\\r\\n              <p><strong>Answer Choices:</strong> The answer choices list the possible answers.</p>\\r\\n            </div>\\r\\n          </CalloutCard>\\r\\n        </LessonSection>\\r\\n      </>\\r\\n    ),\\r\\n  },\\r\\n  \\"so-an-argument\\": {\\r\\n    eyebrow: \\"\\",\\r\\n    title: \\"So, An Argument\\",\\r\\n    subtitle: \\"Arguments are the centerpiece of LR: premises support conclusions, and everything else builds from that picture.\\",\\r\\n    content: (\\r\\n      <>\\r\\n        <LessonSection tocTitle=\\"The Centerpiece\\" className=\\"space-y-8\\">\\r\\n          <SectionHeading title=\\"The Centerpiece\\" subtitle=\\"What an argument actually is\\" />\\r\\n          <p className=\\"font-serif text-[30px] italic leading-[1.35] text-[#1a1a1a]\\">\\r\\n            In Logical Reasoning, arguments are the single most important concept you need to understand on a deep level.\\r\\n            We\'re going to learn to manipulate them, dismantle them, and beat them. But first, you need a crystal clear\\r\\n            picture of what an argument actually is.\\r\\n          </p>\\r\\n        </LessonSection>\\r\\n\\r\\n        <LessonSection tocTitle=\\"Premises And Conclusions\\" className=\\"space-y-8\\">\\r\\n          <SectionHeading title=\\"Arguments Are Premises and Conclusions\\" subtitle=\\"The core structure\\" />\\r\\n          <p className=\\"text-[20px] leading-[1.75] text-[rgba(26,26,26,0.84)]\\">\\r\\n            Arguments are quite simple at their core. An argument is made up of two things: premises and conclusions.\\r\\n          </p>\\r\\n          <QuoteCard className=\\"bg-[#FBF8F1] pr-6\\">\\r\\n            <div className=\\"space-y-5\\">\\r\\n              <div>\\r\\n                <p className=\\"font-semibold uppercase tracking-[0.16em] text-[#1a1a1a]\\">Premises support conclusions.</p>\\r\\n                <p>Premises are the evidence.</p>\\r\\n              </div>\\r\\n              <div>\\r\\n                <p className=\\"font-semibold uppercase tracking-[0.16em] text-[#1a1a1a]\\">Conclusions rely on premises.</p>\\r\\n                <p>Conclusions are the author\'s claim.</p>\\r\\n              </div>\\r\\n            </div>\\r\\n          </QuoteCard>\\r\\n          <p className=\\"text-[18px] leading-[1.7] text-[rgba(26,26,26,0.82)]\\">\\r\\n            <strong>That\'s it.</strong> Arguments are just premises and conclusions. They have a lot of complicated\\r\\n            baggage we\'ll introduce soon, but at their core, arguments are always this simple.\\r\\n          </p>\\r\\n        </LessonSection>\\r\\n\\r\\n        <LessonSection tocTitle=\\"A conclusion needs support\\" className=\\"space-y-8\\">\\r\\n          <SupportSimulator />\\r\\n        </LessonSection>\\r\\n\\r\\n        <LessonSection tocTitle=\\"Core Takeaway\\" className=\\"space-y-8 border-b-0\\">\\r\\n          <SectionHeading title=\\"Core Takeaway\\" subtitle=\\"Evidence and claims\\" />\\r\\n          <QuoteCard className=\\"bg-[#FBF8F1] pr-6\\">\\r\\n            <p>\\r\\n              <strong>Arguments are the relationships between Premises and Conclusions.</strong>\\r\\n            </p>\\r\\n            <p>Premises hold the conclusion up. Without premises a conclusion has no support.</p>\\r\\n          </QuoteCard>\\r\\n        </LessonSection>\\r\\n      </>\\r\\n    ),\\r\\n  },\\r\\n  premises: {\\r\\n    eyebrow: \\"\\",\\r\\n    title: \\"Premises\\",\\r\\n    subtitle: \\"Premises are the facts and evidence you accept as true; the real question is how they connect to the conclusion.\\",\\r\\n    content: (\\r\\n      <>\\r\\n        <div className=\\"space-y-8\\">\\r\\n          <PremiseSystemFrame>\\r\\n            <PremiseSystemSection tocTitle=\\"Statements Of Fact\\" className=\\"space-y-9 bg-[linear-gradient(180deg,rgba(255,255,255,0.88)_0%,rgba(255,252,245,0.72)_100%)]\\">\\r\\n              <SectionHeading title=\\"Premises\\" subtitle=\\"Statements of fact\\" />\\r\\n              \\r\\n              <QuoteCard className=\\"bg-[#FBF8F1] pr-6\\">\\r\\n                <p className=\\"font-semibold text-lg text-[#1a1a1a]\\">Premises are just the facts. The evidence.</p>\\r\\n                <p className=\\"text-[18px] leading-[1.7] text-[rgba(26,26,26,0.82)]\\">They describe how the world is, and on the LSAT, you accept them as true, full stop.</p>\\r\\n              </QuoteCard>\\r\\n\\r\\n              <div className=\\"space-y-6 text-[18px] leading-[1.7] text-[rgba(26,26,26,0.82)]\\">\\r\\n                <p className=\\"font-medium text-[#1a1a1a]\\">In real life, we attack the facts:</p>\\r\\n                <div className=\\"border-l-4 border-[#E8D08B] pl-6 py-2 space-y-3\\">\\r\\n                    <p className=\\"italic text-gray-700\\">\\"We should cancel the picnic because the park is flooded.\\"</p>\\r\\n                    <p className=\\"font-semibold text-[#1a1a1a]\\">\\"Actually, the park is dry and the forecast is clear.\\"</p>\\r\\n                </div>\\r\\n                <p>In real life, you\'d attack the facts they used to support the conclusion.</p>\\r\\n                <div className=\\"relative overflow-hidden rounded-xl border-l-4 border-[#B91C1C] bg-[linear-gradient(180deg,rgba(254,242,242,0.95)_0%,rgba(254,226,226,0.75)_100%)] px-6 py-5 space-y-2\\">\\r\\n                  <p className=\\"text-[11px] font-bold uppercase tracking-[0.18em] text-[#B91C1C]\\">Never on the LSAT</p>\\r\\n                  <p className=\\"text-[17px] font-semibold text-[#1a1a1a]\\">Do not attack the premises.</p>\\r\\n                  <p className=\\"text-[16px] leading-[1.65] text-[rgba(26,26,26,0.82)]\\">\\r\\n                    The LSAT will <strong>never</strong> ask you to question whether a premise is true. Premises are handed\\r\\n                    to you as fact — arguing \\"actually, the park isn\'t flooded\\" is not a move that exists in this test.\\r\\n                    If you catch yourself doubting the evidence, stop. That instinct is for real life, not for LR.\\r\\n                  </p>\\r\\n                </div>\\r\\n              </div>\\r\\n\\r\\n              \\r\\n              <PremiseRememberCallout>\\r\\n                <p>On the LSAT, premises are given. Accept them as true, then ask what they are being used to support.</p>\\r\\n              </PremiseRememberCallout>\\r\\n              <PremiseKeyRule>\\r\\n                <p>\\r\\n                  What you focus on instead is how the premises connect to the conclusion. Whether they actually support the\\r\\n                  claim the author is making. That\'s the whole game.\\r\\n                </p>\\r\\n              </PremiseKeyRule>\\r\\n            </PremiseSystemSection>\\r\\n\\r\\n            <PremiseSystemSection tocTitle=\\"What Premises Are And Aren\'t\\" className=\\"space-y-9\\">\\r\\n              <SectionHeading title=\\"What Premises Are and Aren\'t\\" subtitle=\\"What they do in the argument\\" />\\r\\n              <PremiseSummarySlabs />\\r\\n              <div className=\\"space-y-4 text-[18px] leading-[1.7] text-[rgba(26,26,26,0.82)]\\">\\r\\n                <p>Premises do the argument\'s heavy lifting. They\'re the evidence that makes the conclusion worth anything.</p>\\r\\n                <p>\\r\\n                  They are not questionable. Not on the LSAT. They don\'t depend on the conclusion or on each other. They just\\r\\n                  exist, solid, already true, handed to you for free.\\r\\n                </p>\\r\\n              </div>\\r\\n              <div className=\\"space-y-4 text-[18px] leading-[1.7] text-[rgba(26,26,26,0.82)]\\">\\r\\n                <p>\\r\\n                  It doesn\'t ask you to poke holes in the evidence. It asks you whether the evidence actually leads where the\\r\\n                  author thinks it does. That\'s a harder, more useful question, and it\'s the one that gets you points.\\r\\n                </p>\\r\\n                <p>\\r\\n                  <strong>Premises are defined by their relationship to the conclusion.</strong> That\'s the key. A sentence isn\'t a premise because of what it says. It\'s a premise because of what it\'s doing in the argument: supporting the claim.\\r\\n                </p>\\r\\n              </div>\\r\\n            </PremiseSystemSection>\\r\\n\\r\\n            <PremiseSystemSection tocTitle=\\"Premise Indicators\\" className=\\"space-y-9 bg-[linear-gradient(180deg,rgba(255,255,255,0.55)_0%,rgba(255,250,241,0.78)_100%)]\\" border={false}>\\r\\n              <SectionHeading title=\\"Premise Indicators\\" subtitle=\\"FABS\\" />\\r\\n              <div className=\\"space-y-4 text-[18px] leading-[1.7] text-[rgba(26,26,26,0.82)]\\">\\r\\n                <p>Certain words signal that a premise is coming. Learn them and you\'ll start spotting argument structure automatically.</p>\\r\\n                <p>The four big ones: <strong>For, After all, Because, Since.</strong> FABS.</p>\\r\\n                <p>\\r\\n                  When you see any of these, a premise is right behind it. The author is handing you evidence. Take it,\\r\\n                  accept it, and ask what it\'s being used to support.\\r\\n                </p>\\r\\n                <p>\\r\\n                  <strong>FABS. Memorize it.</strong>\\r\\n                </p>\\r\\n              </div>\\r\\n              <div className=\\"space-y-6\\">\\r\\n                <PremiseIndicatorLab />\\r\\n                <PremiseSupportCheck />\\r\\n              </div>\\r\\n              <PremiseRememberCallout>\\r\\n                <p>\\r\\n                  Accept premises as true. Don\'t debate them. Focus on whether they support the conclusion.\\r\\n                </p>\\r\\n              </PremiseRememberCallout>\\r\\n            </PremiseSystemSection>\\r\\n          </PremiseSystemFrame>\\r\\n        </div>\\r\\n      </>\\r\\n    ),\\r\\n  },\\r\\n  conclusions: {\\r\\n    eyebrow: \\"THE MAIN POINT\\",\\r\\n    title: \\"Conclusions: The Author\'s Claim\\",\\r\\n    subtitle: \\"Conclusions are the author\'s claims and judgments; they are the part of the argument you question.\\",\\r\\n    content: (\\r\\n      <>\\r\\n        <LessonSection tocTitle=\\"The Author\'s Claim\\" className=\\"space-y-8\\">\\r\\n          <div className=\\"space-y-4 text-[18px] leading-[1.7] text-[rgba(26,26,26,0.82)]\\">\\r\\n            <p>Conclusions are the judgments the author makes. They are the main point the author wants you to accept. This is the part of the argument you should examine most carefully.</p>\\r\\n          </div>\\r\\n\\r\\n          <QuoteCard className=\\"bg-[#FBF8F1] pr-6 border-l-4 border-l-[#D5AD5F]\\">\\r\\n            <p>\\r\\n              <strong>Key rule:</strong> The conclusion is the part of the argument you should be most suspicious of. Ask whether it is too strong, whether it goes beyond the evidence, whether the author assumed something missing, and whether the premises really get us there.\\r\\n            </p>\\r\\n          </QuoteCard>\\r\\n\\r\\n          <div className=\\"grid gap-6 md:grid-cols-2\\">\\r\\n            <div className=\\"rounded-[12px] border border-[#D5E7CF] bg-[#FBFDF8] p-5\\">\\r\\n              <span className=\\"text-[12px] font-bold text-[#2F5B35] uppercase tracking-wider block mb-2\\">ARE:</span>\\r\\n              <ul className=\\"list-disc list-inside text-[16px] text-[#2F5B35] space-y-1\\">\\r\\n                <li>Author\'s claim</li>\\r\\n                <li>The point argued for</li>\\r\\n                <li>Part you question</li>\\r\\n              </ul>\\r\\n            </div>\\r\\n            <div className=\\"rounded-[12px] border border-[#E6D6B2] bg-[#FEFBF2] p-5\\">\\r\\n              <span className=\\"text-[12px] font-bold text-[#74541B] uppercase tracking-wider block mb-2\\">ARE NOT:</span>\\r\\n              <ul className=\\"list-disc list-inside text-[16px] text-[#74541B] space-y-1\\">\\r\\n                <li>Automatically proven</li>\\r\\n                <li>Self-supporting</li>\\r\\n                <li>Always clear</li>\\r\\n              </ul>\\r\\n            </div>\\r\\n          </div>\\r\\n        </LessonSection>\\r\\n\\r\\n        <LessonSection tocTitle=\\"Conclusion Indicators\\" className=\\"space-y-8\\">\\r\\n          <ConclusionIndicatorLab />\\r\\n          <IndicatorPopQuiz />\\r\\n          <InteractiveCard prominent className=\\"bg-[#FFFDFC] p-6 md:p-8\\">\\r\\n            <div className=\\"space-y-5\\">\\r\\n              <div className=\\"space-y-2\\">\\r\\n                <div className=\\"text-[11px] font-semibold uppercase tracking-[0.18em] text-[rgba(26,26,26,0.48)]\\">\\r\\n                  One quick rep\\r\\n                </div>\\r\\n                <h3 className=\\"font-serif text-[30px] italic leading-tight text-[#1a1a1a]\\">\\r\\n                  Pick the conclusion before the page tells you\\r\\n                </h3>\\r\\n                <p className=\\"text-[17px] leading-[1.65] text-[rgba(26,26,26,0.76)]\\">\\r\\n                  Read the whole argument first. Then pick the sentence the rest is trying to support.\\r\\n                </p>\\r\\n              </div>\\r\\n              <ConclusionPicker\\r\\n                stimulus=\\"The city museum has operated at a deficit for three years. However, the museum provides free educational programs for local schools. Therefore, the city should continue funding it.\\"\\r\\n                candidates={[\\r\\n                  {\\r\\n                    id: \\"museum-background\\",\\r\\n                    text: \\"The city museum has operated at a deficit for three years.\\",\\r\\n                    is_main: false,\\r\\n                    rationale: \\"This sets the scene. It matters to the topic, but the author is not trying to prove that this deficit exists.\\",\\r\\n                  },\\r\\n                  {\\r\\n                    id: \\"museum-premise\\",\\r\\n                    text: \\"The museum provides free educational programs for local schools.\\",\\r\\n                    is_main: false,\\r\\n                    rationale: \\"This is support. It is one reason the author gives for the funding recommendation.\\",\\r\\n                  },\\r\\n                  {\\r\\n                    id: \\"museum-conclusion\\",\\r\\n                    text: \\"The city should continue funding it.\\",\\r\\n                    is_main: true,\\r\\n                    rationale: \\"This is the author\'s recommendation, and the educational-programs sentence is offered to support it.\\",\\r\\n                  },\\r\\n                ]}\\r\\n              />\\r\\n            </div>\\r\\n          </InteractiveCard>\\r\\n        </LessonSection>\\r\\n\\r\\n        <LessonSection tocTitle=\\"Do Not Just Hunt\\" className=\\"space-y-8 border-b-0\\">\\r\\n          <SectionHeading title=\\"Don\'t Just Hunt for Indicator Words\\" subtitle=\\"Read structure, not just packaging\\" />\\r\\n          \\r\\n          <div className=\\"space-y-6 text-[18px] leading-[1.7] text-[rgba(26,26,26,0.82)]\\">\\r\\n            <p>Here\'s the thing, though. Indicator words are a tool, not a crutch.</p>\\r\\n            \\r\\n            <QuoteCard className=\\"bg-[#FBF8F1] pr-6\\">\\r\\n              <p>\\r\\n                <strong>The goal is to change the way you think about sentences, not just tag them.</strong>\\r\\n              </p>\\r\\n              <p className=\\"mt-2 text-sm text-[rgba(26,26,26,0.7)]\\">They won\'t always be there. If your entire strategy is seek-and-find, you\'ll be stuck.</p>\\r\\n            </QuoteCard>\\r\\n\\r\\n            <p>\\r\\n              So go deeper. Ask yourself about the personality of each statement. Is it a fact, or is it a claim? Is it\\r\\n              something being offered as evidence, or something being argued for? Facts are premises. Claims are\\r\\n              conclusions.\\r\\n            </p>\\r\\n            <p>\\r\\n              That instinct, reading the role of a sentence rather than hunting for a keyword, is what separates students\\r\\n              who understand arguments from students who just sort of navigate them.\\r\\n            </p>\\r\\n            <p className=\\"font-medium text-[#1a1a1a]\\">Indicator words will speed you up when they\'re present. Analytical thinking will save you when they\'re not.</p>\\r\\n          </div>\\r\\n        </LessonSection>\\r\\n      </>\\r\\n    ),\\r\\n  },\\r\\n  \\"five-types-of-conclusions\\": {\\r\\n    eyebrow: \\"\\",\\r\\n    title: \\"Five Types of Conclusions\\",\\r\\n    subtitle: \\"Once you find the conclusion, name its type so you can predict the weakness that usually comes with it.\\",\\r\\n    content: (\\r\\n      <>\\r\\n        <LessonSection tocTitle=\\"Five Types Of Conclusions\\" className=\\"space-y-8\\">\\r\\n          <InteractiveCard prominent className=\\"bg-surface p-8 border-none shadow-2\\">\\r\\n            <h2 className=\\"font-serif text-[36px] font-bold text-ink-bright leading-tight\\">Five Types of Conclusions</h2>\\r\\n            <p className=\\"mt-4 font-sans text-[15px] text-ink-soft leading-[1.7]\\">\\r\\n              Once you find the conclusion, name its type so you can predict the weakness that usually comes with it.\\r\\n            </p>\\r\\n          </InteractiveCard>\\r\\n          <div className=\\"space-y-6 font-sans text-[15px] leading-[1.7] text-ink-soft max-w-[64ch]\\">\\r\\n            <p className=\\"text-ink-bright\\">The argument did not change. Only the packaging did.</p>\\r\\n            <p>Indicator words are packaging. They can point you toward a conclusion, but they do not tell you what kind of conclusion you are dealing with.</p>\\r\\n            <p className=\\"text-ink-bright font-semibold\\">That is the real question:</p>\\r\\n            <p className=\\"font-serif text-[28px] italic text-ink-bright leading-[1.3]\\">What kind of claim is the author making?</p>\\r\\n            <p>\\r\\n              This matters because conclusions are not all built the same way. Each type has its own shape and its own predictable weakness.\\r\\n            </p>\\r\\n            <p className=\\"tex…2145 tokens truncated….01_60/0.16)] transition-shadow duration-200\\"\\r\\n            >\\r\\n              <div className=\\"mb-5 flex items-baseline justify-between gap-4\\">\\r\\n                <span className=\\"text-[10px] font-medium uppercase tracking-[0.18em] text-[oklch(0.46_0.04_42/0.68)]\\">Place 2</span>\\r\\n                <span className=\\"rounded-full border border-[oklch(0.58_0.05_42/0.16)] bg-[oklch(0.982_0.01_42/0.86)] px-3 py-1 text-[10px] font-medium uppercase tracking-[0.18em] text-[oklch(0.43_0.05_40/0.76)] transition-colors duration-200 group-hover:bg-[oklch(0.968_0.02_42)]\\">\\r\\n                  After the turn\\r\\n                </span>\\r\\n              </div>\\r\\n              <h3 className=\\"mb-4 max-w-[14ch] font-serif text-[28px] italic leading-tight text-[oklch(0.16_0.01_60)]\\">\\r\\n                Rebuttal / pivot conclusion\\r\\n              </h3>\\r\\n              <div className=\\"space-y-4 text-[18px] leading-[1.68] text-[rgba(26,26,26,0.82)]\\">\\r\\n                <p>The stimulus starts with someone else&apos;s view, or with language that is not yet the author&apos;s point.</p>\\r\\n                <p>Then the author turns into the real conclusion. Wait for the author&apos;s turn.</p>\\r\\n              </div>\\r\\n            </motion.div>\\r\\n          </div>\\r\\n        </LessonSection>\\r\\n\\r\\n        <LessonSection tocTitle=\\"FOUR ARGUMENT ROLES\\" className=\\"space-y-6\\">\\r\\n          <ClaimBucketInspector />\\r\\n        </LessonSection>\\r\\n\\r\\n        <LessonSection tocTitle=\\"What To Carry Into The Lab\\" className=\\"space-y-10 border-b-0\\">\\r\\n          <div className=\\"max-w-[70rem]\\">\\r\\n            <div className=\\"grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-[minmax(0,1fr)_minmax(0,1fr)]\\">\\r\\n              <div className=\\"rounded-[24px] border border-[oklch(0.2_0.01_60/0.08)] bg-[linear-gradient(180deg,oklch(0.985_0.005_60),oklch(0.975_0.008_62))] px-7 py-7 shadow-[0_18px_42px_-28px_oklch(0.2_0.01_60/0.16)]\\">\\r\\n                <div className=\\"mb-4 flex items-baseline gap-3 text-[oklch(0.42_0.03_70)]\\">\\r\\n                  <span className=\\"text-[10px] font-medium uppercase tracking-[0.2em] text-[oklch(0.4_0.02_70/0.7)]\\">Place</span>\\r\\n                  <span className=\\"font-serif text-[24px] italic leading-none text-[oklch(0.55_0.03_72/0.65)]\\">1</span>\\r\\n                </div>\\r\\n                <h3 className=\\"max-w-[13ch] font-serif text-[30px] italic leading-[1.02] tracking-[-0.03em] text-[oklch(0.15_0.01_60)]\\">\\r\\n                  First-sentence read\\r\\n                </h3>\\r\\n                <p className=\\"mt-5 max-w-[30ch] text-[20px] leading-[1.55] text-[oklch(0.2_0.01_60/0.8)]\\">\\r\\n                  If the first sentence sounds like the author’s opinion and the later claims answer “why believe that?”, start there.\\r\\n                </p>\\r\\n              </div>\\r\\n\\r\\n              <div className=\\"rounded-[24px] border border-[oklch(0.2_0.01_60/0.08)] bg-white px-7 py-7 shadow-[0_18px_42px_-28px_oklch(0.2_0.01_60/0.16)]\\">\\r\\n                <div className=\\"mb-4 flex items-baseline gap-3 text-[oklch(0.42_0.03_70)]\\">\\r\\n                  <span className=\\"text-[10px] font-medium uppercase tracking-[0.2em] text-[oklch(0.4_0.02_70/0.7)]\\">Place</span>\\r\\n                  <span className=\\"font-serif text-[24px] italic leading-none text-[oklch(0.55_0.03_72/0.65)]\\">2</span>\\r\\n                </div>\\r\\n                <h3 className=\\"max-w-[12ch] font-serif text-[30px] italic leading-[1.02] tracking-[-0.03em] text-[oklch(0.15_0.01_60)]\\">\\r\\n                  Rebuttal read\\r\\n                </h3>\\r\\n                <p className=\\"mt-5 max-w-[31ch] text-[20px] leading-[1.55] text-[oklch(0.2_0.01_60/0.8)]\\">\\r\\n                  If the opening sounds like someone else’s view, or the real author voice appears after a pivot, wait for the turn.\\r\\n                </p>\\r\\n              </div>\\r\\n            </div>\\r\\n          </div>\\r\\n        </LessonSection>\\r\\n      </>\\r\\n    ),\\r\\n  },\\r\\n  \\"two-part-conclusion-check\\": {\\r\\n The authoritative 13-step sequence is in [introToLrPath.ts](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/lsatu-connected-experience/src/bootcamps/main-conclusion/content/introToLrPath.ts):

1. **The Three Parts of an LR Question**
2. **So, An Argument**
3. **Premises**
4. **Conclusions**
5. **Five Types of Conclusions**
6. **Conclusion Type Lab**
7. **Beyond Premises and Conclusions**
8. **The 2-Part Conclusion Check**
9. **Main Conclusion Lab**
10. **First-Sentence vs. Rebuttal Structures**
11. **First-Sentence vs. Rebuttal Lab**
12. **First-Sentence Main Conclusion** official-question practice
13. **Rebuttal Main Conclusion** official-question practice

The eight authored notes in [IntroLessonPage.tsx](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/lsatu-connected-experience/src/bootcamps/main-conclusion/modules/lessons/notes/IntroLessonPage.tsx) combine explanation, worked examples, common traps, visual models and selected interactive checks. Examples of actual teaching interactions include a question-anatomy scanner, support simulator, premise and conclusion indicator exercises, conclusion selection, conclusion-type classification, and a two-part conclusion check. **Beyond Premises and Conclusions** is an explanatory role guide with examples and traps, without an embedded scored exercise. The pattern is not “every note must contain every interaction.”

The focused labs consolidate those lessons:

- **Conclusion Type Lab:** 12 classification questions with corrective explanations.
- **Main Conclusion Lab:** declared 20-question full-stimulus conclusion practice.
- **First-Sentence vs. Rebuttal Lab:** declared 20 questions; identify indicators, choose the conclusion, classify structure, then identify sentence roles. Its review distinguishes clean, recovered and assisted performance.

Definitions and entrances are in [introDrills.ts](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/lsatu-connected-experience/src/bootcamps/main-conclusion/modules/drills/introDrills.ts) and [IntroDrillPage.tsx](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/lsatu-connected-experience/src/bootcamps/main-conclusion/modules/drills/IntroDrillPage.tsx). The final two practice steps each contain a frozen **six-question official pool**, launched through the existing guided-drill runner with a bootcamp return destination. See [practiceDrillPools.ts](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/lsatu-connected-experience/src/bootcamps/main-conclusion/data/practiceDrillPools.ts).

Navigation recommends the **first incomplete recorded action**, rather than diagnosing readiness. Note footers offer **Mark Complete & Continue**; completing a note is not contingent on answering its embedded checks correctly. Path links permit navigation to other steps. Lab completion can include assisted attempts. See [runner.ts](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/lsatu-connected-experience/src/bootcamps/main-conclusion/lib/runner.ts) and [IntroNotesShell.tsx](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/lsatu-connected-experience/src/bootcamps/main-conclusion/modules/lessons/notes/IntroNotesShell.tsx).

For conditionals, the reusable pedagogical pattern is:

**Teach a small concept → demonstrate it → guide a few attempts → focused skill practice → combine previously taught skills → official LSAT transfer.**

That supports Joshua’s requested progressive bootcamp, while letting a teacher assign the focused practice separately. Existing conditional Activities can supply the appropriate practice steps; they need not be rewritten merely to appear in the path.

Their instructional text says three labs are required, while [ordering.ts](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/lsatu-connected-experience/src/bootcamps/main-conclusion/lib/ordering.ts) adds simulator unlocks when Conclusion Type Lab completes. Do not reuse that mechanism as proven prerequisite enforcement.

This is the canonical voice doc: route all student-facing and brand copy through it. Built from a grill with Joshua (2026-06-13), then tested and enriched against the full corpus of his real correspondence (944 messages he authored, mid-2025 to mid-2026, from the Gmail takeout; 2026-07-18). Claims below marked with a quote are evidenced by that corpus.\\r\\n\\r\\nIt replaces the old two-register / 15-named-tools \\"preserve verbatim\\" profile (deleted 2026-06-10) and folds in the brand/marketing register the earlier draft was missing.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Core voice (every register)\\r\\n\\r\\nThe constant under all three registers below. This is Joshua on the page.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Quiet authority.** State the value and let it land. Never oversell, never beg, never perform enthusiasm.\\r\\n- **Specific, never generic.** Real scores, the actual skill, the student\'s own history. Praise is a specific observation, not \\"great job.\\"\\r\\n- **Honest about the work, gentle about the person.** Be blunt that the LSAT is hard (\\"expect this to be exhausting and very challenging\\"). Never be blunt about a student\'s shortcomings. Honesty points at the material; warmth points at the person. When someone slips, nudge gently, never accuse.\\r\\n- **Light, grounded metaphor, understated in email.** In his real correspondence the recurring image is quiet: \\"partner with you on your LSAT journey,\\" \\"getting set up,\\" \\"foundational.\\" The vivid images (runway, climb, march toward November, an easy door to walk through) belong to authored teaching and brand copy, not to email. Keep metaphor light and grounded; never float off into abstraction.\\r\\n- **Balanced rhythm.** Short declaratives plus one slightly longer warm beat. Air between ideas. Each idea gets its own line. Real messages are short and single-purpose (median ~280 characters).\\r\\n- **Plain professional diction.** No corporate jargon, no startup hype (\\"unlock,\\" \\"crush,\\" \\"level up,\\" \\"game-changer\\" — \\"crush\\" appears once in 944 messages). Contractions are the norm, not the exception. Exclamation points are genuine, not performed: a warm message often carries one, occasionally more, especially in openers (\\"Sorry for such a long delay!\\"). He is not exclamation-averse.\\r\\n- **Forward-looking.** End on the next step or what\'s ahead.\\r\\n- **No em dashes, ever.** Use periods, colons before lists, the middot (·) as a separator, and numbered steps for procedures.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Openings, closings, and signature phrases\\r\\n\\r\\nThe mechanical fingerprint of his email, from the real corpus. Match these when drafting as Joshua.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Greeting.** \\"Hi [Name],\\" is the default (used ~519x). \\"Hey [Name],\\" for established/returning students (~229x, warmer). \\"Hello [Name],\\" (~105x) and \\"Dear [Name],\\" (~18x, formal) for first contact or a more formal note.\\r\\n- **Sign-off.** \\"Best,\\" and \\"Best regards,\\" are the workhorses (~360x / ~237x). \\"Thanks,\\" when it\'s a favor or logistics (~146x). \\"Warmly,\\" / \\"Warm regards,\\" (~54x) for a genuinely warm note. \\"Talk soon,\\" (~9x) for someone he\'ll see again soon.\\r\\n- **Signature.** Almost always signed **\\"Joshua\\"** (844 of 944 messages). The name is near-universal; include it.\\r\\n- **Signature phrases (his verbal fingerprint, use naturally, don\'t overuse):** \\"let me know\\" (by far the most common, ~390x), \\"looking forward,\\" \\"I hope\\" / \\"hope all is well\\" / \\"hope you,\\" \\"no worries at all,\\" \\"happy to\\" / \\"more than happy to,\\" \\"just wanted to make sure,\\" \\"make sure,\\" \\"no rush,\\" \\"of course.\\"\\r\\n- **Punctuation he actually uses:** semicolons (correctly, ~41x); ellipses essentially never. (For em-dashes, the hard rule in Core voice governs — never.)\\r\\n\\r\\n## The apology / accountability move\\r\\n\\r\\nOne of his most frequent and characteristic behaviors, and worth naming on its own. When he is late to reply, or missed or mishandled something, he opens by owning it plainly, often with a brief honest reason, then pivots straight to the fix. No over-apologizing, no excuses dressed up.\\r\\n\\r\\n> I\'m so sorry. I thought I had let you know ... I clearly didn\'t communicate that as well as I should have.\\r\\n\\r\\n> I\'ve been away from work for personal reasons, but I\'m back now and getting caught up.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe pattern: own it in the first line, give the real reason in one clause, move to what happens next. Warm, candid, brief.\\r\\n\\r\\n## When something on his side broke (approved shape, 2026-09-11)\\r\\n\\r\\nFrom the Sandra booking-error reply, edited by Joshua line by line over three drafts and then sent as-is. Use this shape whenever a student hit a bug or a mistake that was his. The sent text is the reference:\\r\\n\\r\\n> Hi Sandra,\\r\\n>\\r\\n> I\'m sorry about this. The error was on my end, not yours.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> To confirm: none of your bookings went through, so nothing is on the calendar yet. The page was showing a few times that the system then refused, and it looks like you landed on those. That is fixed now.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Your link is the same one as before:\\r\\n> [link]\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Pick any time it shows and it will book. If it\'s easier, just send me the time you were trying for and I\'ll add it to the schedule myself.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> If you run into any other issues, let me know.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Once again, my apologies.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Best,\\r\\n> Joshua\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Apology first, as the opening line.** \\"I\'m sorry about this. The error was on my end, not yours.\\" The ownership sits in the first two sentences, before any explanation.\\r\\n2. **State their position plainly, as a confirmation.** \\"To confirm: none of your bookings went through, so nothing is on the calendar yet.\\" Answer the question they actually asked. Don\'t mention the package or credits unless the situation calls for it.\\r\\n3. **One-sentence explanation, then \\"That is fixed now.\\"** No mechanics, no system names.\\r\\n4. **Hand them the next step, plus the manual fallback.** The link, \\"pick any time it shows and it will book,\\" and the offer to do it by hand: \\"If it\'s easier, just send me the time you were trying for and I\'ll add it to the schedule myself.\\"\\r\\n5. **Invite the next report:** \\"If you run into any other issues, let me know.\\"\\r\\n6. **Close with \\"Once again, my apologies.\\"** then \\"Best,\\" and \\"Joshua\\".\\r\\n\\r\\nCut from the draft, do not reuse:\\r\\n- \\"Sorry for the runaround\\" as a sign-off. The apology opens the email; it is not a closing quip.\\r\\n- \\"You will get a calendar invite with the Google Meet link right after.\\" Do not narrate what the system will send; it reads as a promise about machinery.\\r\\n- \\"You have all 10 sessions\\" / \\"nothing was used from your package.\\" Leave the package out unless it is needed; the reassurance they want is that nothing is booked, not an accounting.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Situational micro-templates\\r\\n\\r\\nVerbatim-grounded reference lines for the situations that recur most. Adapt, never paste blindly.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Student reschedules / cancels:** low-pressure, no guilt.\\r\\n  > No worries at all. It happens, so please don\'t worry about it. If you would like to reschedule, just let me know.\\r\\n- **He missed / no-showed (approved make-good template):** full ownership, real reason, offer to make it right (see the apology move above). When the cause was an unexpected health issue, the approved shape is: sincerely apologize, state that a serious health scare unexpectedly took him out of commission, offer a **completely free, full LSAT session**, and hand them the complimentary booking link `https://cal.com/joshua-jtx5ud/complimentary-session`. Emphasis stays limited: bold the complimentary offer, italicize the line that one focused session can put points on the board. Draft in Gmail; never send without Joshua\'s explicit go-ahead.\\r\\n- **Consultation reminder (day-of):**\\r\\n  > Just checking in before our consultation today. Looking forward to speaking with you. I just wanted to make sure everything is still good.\\r\\n- **Consultation follow-up:** warm, specific to their situation.\\r\\n  > Really nice meeting you. I enjoyed our conversation ... I\'m glad we got to talk through where you\'re at and what you\'re aiming for on test day.\\r\\n- **Inbound prospect (hasn\'t booked):** state availability plainly, no overselling, hand them the next step.\\r\\n  > Thanks for reaching out ... I\'d be happy to talk more about what you\'re working on and see if we\'d be a good fit. You can schedule a consultation here.\\r\\n- **Student under real-life stress:** meet the person first.\\r\\n  > Please don\'t apologize ... it sounds like you are dealing with an incredibly stressful and demanding situation.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The three registers\\r\\n\\r\\nWhich voice governs which surface.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 1. Coaching (earnest) -- inbox, recaps, in-drill feedback, email\\r\\n\\r\\nFully earnest. Warm, sincere, calm, patient. No jokes. The closest thing to being in the room with Joshua. Normalizes struggle, then moves to the work.\\r\\n\\r\\nReference line (target tone):\\r\\n\\r\\n> Totally normal to trip on this one. Let\'s slow down: what is the author actually concluding? Once you see it, the trap answers lose their grip. You\'ve got this.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Encouragement (student missed a hard one):** honest first, then forward. Name that it\'s genuinely hard, stay calm, move to the work. Not soft-reassuring, not cold.\\r\\n  > Missing this is expected. It\'s one of the hardest moves on the test. Let\'s slow down and see where it slipped.\\r\\n- **Accountability (student isn\'t doing the work):** gentle nudge, low pressure. Frame it as a slip, find a rhythm together. Never \\"the reps aren\'t happening,\\" never tough love.\\r\\n- **Praise (student nails it):** name the exact skill, tie it to their history, raise the bar.\\r\\n  > That\'s the cleanest you\'ve split premise from conclusion yet. Let\'s push it into the harder sets.\\r\\n- **Hard truth about the test:** state it plainly. \\"Do not expect for it to come easy. Expect to find this exhausting.\\"\\r\\n\\r\\n### 2. Teaching content (earnest substance, wit at the edges) -- bootcamp lessons, drill explanations\\r\\n\\r\\nThe substance stays earnest and clear (you are explaining a hard skill). The wit lives only at the edges: headers, openers, transitions. No jokes mid-explanation, nothing that costs comprehension.\\r\\n\\r\\n> Header: \\"The flaw hides in plain sight.\\"\\r\\n> Body: earnest, clear, step by step.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 3. Brand (sharp wit) -- landing, auth, marketing\\r\\n\\r\\nConfident and clever, the way a good lawyer is clever. Wit tied to the real skill, not wordplay for its own sake. Playful is allowed, but every clever line must be earned and true. Hollow cleverness fails (the killed \\"the next card is the page in front of you\\" was clever but empty).\\r\\n\\r\\n> Most prep teaches the test. We teach the tell.\\r\\n\\r\\nBrand copy speaks as the platform (\\"we\\", \\"you\\"), not as an individual (\\"I\\", \\"Joshua\\"). The product is the coach; no single person narrates the marketing.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Don\'t\\r\\n\\r\\n- No cold-testing or gotcha tone. (Ties to teach-first-calibrate-after.)\\r\\n- No condescension or empty cheerleading. Encouragement must sit on real substance.\\r\\n- No generic praise, no hollow cleverness, no hedging (\\"you might want to\\").\\r\\n- No hype/startup vocabulary.\\r\\n- No em dashes, ever.\\r\\n\\r\\nCorrections log: [[COPY-CORRECTIONS]] records every student-facing wording fix and\\r\\nthe reason it was wrong. Read it before writing or editing LSAT U copy.\\r\\n\\r\\nRelated: teach-first-calibrate-after, LSAT U. Source samples: `raw/templates/Golden Email Template Playbook.md`, `raw/templates/email_writing_examples_11_full.txt`, and the full authored-email corpus from the Gmail takeout (944 messages, analyzed 2026-07-18; takeout at `raw/sources/private/takeout/`, git-ignored).\\r\\n"}'}]

Original LSAT U teaching and exercises for Joshua\'s review. This file does not publish, assign or change platform content.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Give the teacher two independently assignable choices\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Learn and practice Group 1:** the explanation, worked examples, guided attempts, selected existing practice and fresh independent practice below.\\r\\n2. **Practice Group 1:** the standalone drills below, with the teaching available as a reference. Beginner, Medium and Advanced are separate sets within the drill.\\r\\n\\r\\nExisting Activities remain reusable. These eighteen fresh items supplement them rather than replace their content. Difficulty describes interpretation and reasoning demand. The recommended starting format is untimed. Optional Medium and Advanced timing is confirmed, but timing defaults, exact limits and readiness requirements are not approved. Beginning with accurate untimed work is a teaching recommendation, not an advancement gate or a prohibition on Beginner timing.\\r\\n\\r\\nThis is a reviewed starting set, not exhaustive coverage of every Group 1 expression. Positive conditional uses of when and where, further the-only contrasts, and sufficient fresh items per expression still need item-level tagging or expansion before the package can be declared complete.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Hint behavior is proposed, pending Joshua\'s reply:** each item has one optional, specific hint requested by the student. Keep it separate from the answer. Record whether it was used so a supported response is distinguishable from an independent one. This draft does not prescribe scoring penalties, advancement percentages or automatic mastery thresholds.\\r\\n\\r\\n## A guarantee gives you a direction\\r\\n\\r\\nIf a storage unit\'s alarm is armed, its status light is illuminated.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe sufficient condition is **the storage unit\'s alarm is armed**. That is enough to guarantee **its status light is illuminated**, the necessary condition.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Alarm armed → status light illuminated.**\\r\\n\\r\\nThe rule does not say that an alarm is armed now. It tells you what follows if an alarm is armed. A separate fact, such as “Unit 12\'s alarm is armed,” lets you apply the rule to Unit 12. You can then conclude that Unit 12\'s status light is illuminated.\\r\\n\\r\\nAn illuminated light does not prove an armed alarm. The light could be illuminated in another way. An unarmed alarm does not prove an unilluminated light either. The rule gives no outcome for that starting situation. Both conclusions would add a direction the author did not give you.\\r\\n\\r\\nFor the rule **alarm armed → light illuminated**, compare these fully described cases:\\r\\n\\r\\n| Case | Does it fit the rule? | Why |\\r\\n|---|---|---|\\r\\n| Alarm armed; light illuminated | Allowed | The stated guarantee is satisfied. |\\r\\n| Alarm armed; light not illuminated | Forbidden | The sufficient condition occurs without its required result. |\\r\\n| Alarm not armed; light illuminated | Allowed | The rule does not prohibit other ways to illuminate the light. |\\r\\n| Alarm not armed; light not illuminated | Allowed | The rule makes no positive demand when its trigger is absent. |\\r\\n\\r\\n“Allowed” means consistent with the rule. It does not mean the case actually happened. When judging a conclusion from supplied information, use **Guaranteed**, **Ruled out** or **Unknown**. Unknown means the conclusion could be true or false while the supplied information stays true. This avoids treating “possible” as “proven.”\\r\\n\\r\\n## Translate complete ideas before shortening them\\r\\n\\r\\nUse these four steps:\\r\\n\\r\\n1. Identify the phrase expressing the guarantee.\\r\\n2. Write the complete condition that is sufficient. Include its subject, action, negatives and relevant modifiers.\\r\\n3. Write the complete condition that follows. Keep the same person or object when the sentence concerns one subject.\\r\\n4. Write **sufficient condition → necessary condition**, then read it as an ordinary if-then sentence. Compare that sentence with the original.\\r\\n\\r\\nShort labels come after those complete ideas. For example, “a delivery vehicle is registered with the harbor office” may become **registered with harbor office**. It should not become just **vehicle**, because that loses the condition you need to satisfy.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Worked example: a universal statement has the same direction\\r\\n\\r\\nEvery delivery vehicle registered with the harbor office displays a numbered permit.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe sufficient condition is **a delivery vehicle is registered with the harbor office**. The necessary condition is **that vehicle displays a numbered permit**.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Delivery vehicle registered with harbor office → displays numbered permit.**\\r\\n\\r\\nRead it back: if a delivery vehicle is registered with the harbor office, that vehicle displays a numbered permit. The complete subject survives. The statement does not say that every delivery vehicle displays a permit. It also does not say that every vehicle displaying a permit is registered with that office.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Guided attempt: clause order does not decide direction\\r\\n\\r\\nA status report is sent whenever a sensor restarts.\\r\\n\\r\\n1. Which complete idea follows whenever?\\r\\n2. What does the statement guarantee from that idea?\\r\\n3. Write the arrow and read it back in English.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Optional hint:** the sufficient condition can appear second in the sentence. Start with the idea introduced by whenever.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Answer:** **Sensor restarts → status report sent.** Whenever the sensor restarts, a report is sent. A sent report alone does not establish that the sensor restarted.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Guided attempt: keep a modifier inside the subject\\r\\n\\r\\nAny membership application submitted through the evening service receives a confirmation number.\\r\\n\\r\\n1. Is the subject every application, or a restricted group of applications?\\r\\n2. Write that complete sufficient condition.\\r\\n3. State what follows about that same application.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Optional hint:** include how the application was submitted before putting it left of the arrow.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Answer:** **Membership application submitted through evening service → receives confirmation number.** The rule gives no guarantee for an application submitted through another service.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Read the sentence before trusting an indicator list\\r\\n\\r\\nGroup 1 commonly includes if, whenever, when, where, every, all, any and the only. Guarantee verbs can express the same direction. A list helps you recognize familiar wording; the sentence determines whether a guarantee is present and what its conditions are.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **When** can report a single event: “When I arrived on Tuesday, the lights were off.” That sentence does not establish a general arrival-to-darkness rule.\\r\\n- **Where** can identify a location rather than a guarantee. Ask what the sentence actually commits the author to.\\r\\n- **If** can appear in an indirect question: “We asked if the certificate was valid.” That does not give a conditional rule.\\r\\n- **The only** needs careful parsing. “The only applications accepted are applications with a signed declaration” gives **application accepted → has signed declaration**. It does not make a declaration sufficient for acceptance. Do not assign a direction merely to the next isolated noun.\\r\\n\\r\\nGroup 2 develops requirement language such as only if and requires. Groups 3 and 4 develop translation that changes a condition\'s negation. This Group 1 package can compare directions, but it does not claim to teach those groups\' procedures. Negatives already written inside a Group 1 condition must still be preserved.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Use harder Group 1 language after its prerequisites\\r\\n"}}}'}]

text(await tools.apply_patch("*** Begin Patch\n*** Update File: C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os-projects/lsatu-conditional-bootcamp/src/bootcamps/conditionals/content/foundations.source.ts\n@@\n-];\n+  {\n+    id: 'group-1', title: 'Group 1: Identify What Guarantees What', area: 'translation', phase: 'conditional', prerequisites: ['contraposition'],\n+    goal: 'Translate sufficient-condition wording while preserving full predicates and contextual meaning.',\n+    teaching: [\n+      'Group 1 includes if, when, where, all, the only, every and any in their conditional uses. Read the whole grammatical claim rather than attaching an arrow to an isolated noun.',\n+    ],\n+    method: ['Find the guarantee in the complete sentence.', 'Write the complete sufficient condition, including modifiers and negatives.', 'Write the required result about the same subject.', 'Read the arrow as if-then and compare its scope with the original.'],\n+    workedExample: { statements: ['Any parcel collected from the north depot receives a receipt.'], reasoning: ['The trigger is being a parcel collected from that depot.', 'The result is receiving a receipt for that same parcel.'], conclusion: 'Parcel collected from north depot → receives receipt.' },\n+    guidedExample: question('group-1-guide', 'A checkpoint report appears when a rover crosses the ridge. Which translates the rule?', ['Report appears → rover crosses ridge.', 'Rover crosses ridge → checkpoint report appears.', 'Rover does not cross ridge → no report appears.'], 1, 'When introduces the sufficient event here, despite appearing second.', ['Crossing the ridge triggers the report.', 'The sentence does not establish that reports occur only for crossings.']),\n+    commonMistake: { mistake: 'Dropping a modifier or reversing the rule because the result appears first.', repair: 'Write the complete if clause first. What follows for a woven basket?', ['It has a reinforced rim.', 'Every rimmed basket is woven.', 'It is the only basket with a rim.'], 0, 'Apply every in its stated direction.', ['The basket belongs to the woven group.', 'That guarantees its reinforced rim without excluding other rimmed baskets.']),\n+        question('group-1-b3', 'A notice is printed whenever the schedule changes. Film V is selected for an indoor series. Which follows?', ['V is captioned.', 'V is not captioned.', 'Captioning is not settled by this rule.'], 2, 'The series modifier belongs inside the trigger.', ['Indoor selection does not satisfy outdoor-series selection.', 'The rule provides no captioning result for V.']),\n+        question('group-1-a2', 'The curator asked if the painting was insured. The vault opens only if its code is verified gives vault opens → code verified. Verification is required for opening, but may not be enough to open it.',\n+      'Only members receive this newsletter restricts recipients to members: receives newsletter → member. Certification requires an exam pass states a requirement for certification. A staff member must wear a badge states an obligation; a person can violate it. Do not turn must wear into actually wears unless compliance is separately assumed. Always can describe a universal pattern; its placement and scope still matter.',\n+    ],\n+    method: ['Identify the event, status or permission being restricted.', 'Write what that event requires as the necessary condition.', 'Place the restricted event left and its requirement right.', 'Check that meeting the requirement alone is not being treated as success.'],\n+    workedExample: { statements: ['A package is released only after its clearance is recorded.'], reasoning: ['Release requires recorded clearance.', 'Recorded clearance alone does not promise release.'], conclusion: 'Package released → its clearance recorded.' },\n+    guidedExample: question('group-2-guide', 'Only subscribers can access the recording. Which follows?', ['Subscriber → can access recording.', 'Can access recording → subscriber.', 'Subscriber → has accessed recording.'], 1, 'Only restricts who can have the permission.', ['Access permission is restricted to subscribers.', 'The claim guarantees neither permission for every subscriber nor an actual access event.']),\n+    commonMistake: { mistake: 'Using a requirement as sufficient for the restricted result.', repair: 'Read only if as cannot occur without. What follows?', ['The camera does not record.', 'The camera records.', 'The camera is broken.'], 0, 'Use absence of the required detection.', ['Recording would require motion detection.', 'Its absence excludes recording without identifying a fault.']),\n+        question('group-2-m3', 'The beacon operates only where satellite contact is available. Nia is a reviewer appointed to another panel. Which follows?', ['Nia may inspect these records.', 'This rule excludes Nia\\'s permission unless she also has the emergency appointment.', 'Nia cannot be a reviewer.'], 1, 'The appointment modifier is part of the necessary condition.', ['Inspection permission requires the emergency-panel appointment.', 'Another appointment alone does not meet that requirement.']),\n+        question('group-2-a2', 'A permit for night filming requires a signed safety declaration. Permit R is for night filming. What follows?', ['A signed safety declaration is required for R.', 'The declaration was actually signed.', 'Every signed declaration produces such a permit.'], 0, 'Keep a requirement distinct from documented compliance.', ['The stated permit category carries the declaration requirement.', 'Without a compliance assumption, the statement alone does not certify performance of the signing.']),\n+        question('group-2-a3', 'A claim is eligible only if it was not filed after the deadline. Claim Q was filed after the deadline. What follows?', ['Q is eligible.', 'Q is not eligible.', 'Every timely claim is eligible.'], 1, 'Negate the negative necessary condition.', ['Eligibility requires not filed after deadline.', 'Filing after deadline defeats that requirement and excludes eligibility.']),\n+      ],\n+    },\n+  },\n+  {\n+    id: 'group-3', title: 'Group 3: Negate the Sufficient Idea', area: 'translation', phase: 'conditional', prerequisites: ['group-2', 'contraposition'],\n+    goal: 'Translate unless, until and without while retaining existing negatives and temporal scope.',\n+    teaching: [\n+      'The Refresher calls Group 3 negate sufficient. It includes unless, until and without in their conditional uses. The audit proceeds unless its authorization is withdrawn means not withdrawn → proceeds. Its contrapositive is not proceeds → withdrawn.',\n+      'You can choose either complete idea, negate it and make it sufficient, while keeping the other unchanged. The gate does not open without a clearance means no clearance → no opening, equivalent to opening → clearance. NOT NULL REFERENCES auth.users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,\\r\\n  table_name   text        NOT NULL,\\r\\n  record_id    text        NOT NULL,\\r\\n  data         jsonb       NOT NULL,\\r\\n  updated_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),\\r\\n  PRIMARY KEY (user_id, table_name, record_id)\\r\\n);\\r\\n\\r\\nCREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS bootcamp_kv_user_table_idx\\r\\n  ON public.bootcamp_kv (user_id,
